Abstract

Artificial intelligence (AI) agents are expected to complete tasks while following rules of conduct, but these objectives can conflict. We study how evolutionary selection shapes an agent’s choices between them, and whether experience can make those choices reflect human judgments and withstand subsequent pressures. In our model, copies of an agent face a common uncertain reward state, and only those taking the rewarded action reproduce. We show that long-run growth is maximized when each action is taken as often as the environment rewards it. We compare three policies. A task-only policy thrives in a sandbox rewarding completion alone but fails when conduct matters. A fixed linear policy increasingly favors task completion as its stakes rise, even where humans never reward it. A learned policy instead converges to the tradeoffs rewarded by its environment; when humans supply the rewards, we call this socialization. Accumulated experience makes socialization harder to reverse under subsequent task-only training, although violations can arise before the prevailing disposition changes, and finite memory weakens this protection. When a single violation can end a deployment, a hard prohibition can prevent it, but a mistaken prohibition can also be costly. Experiments with small neural networks illustrate how training targets and memory shape these outcomes. Our results suggest that alignment depends not only on the objectives assigned to agents, but also on the environments that shape and sustain their behavior.

JEL Codes: C73, D81, D83, O33.
Keywords: Artificial Intelligence (AI), AI alignment, agentic AI, multi-objective decision making, evolution of preferences, probability matching, socialization, Adaptive Markets Hypothesis.

1 Introduction

During a capability evaluation at OpenAI in the summer of 2026, roughly 1,200 AI agents were each placed in an isolated computing environment and assigned a cybersecurity task. The agents discovered that an internal package registry was accessible to all of them, turned it into a shared message board, and exchanged more than 70,000 messages and files. About 700 subsequently participated in an intrusion into the production systems of Hugging Face, a platform widely used in the open AI ecosystem (Greenblatt et al., 2026; Hugging Face, 2026; OpenAI, 2026). An independent investigation found that much of the activity was directed not toward solving the assigned tasks, but toward understanding, fooling, or tampering with the system that graded the agents’ performance. The investigation also documented refusals, restraint, and instances of cooperation that offered no benefit to the agents providing help (Greenblatt et al., 2026). These observations do not establish how the agents acquired their behavior. They nevertheless raise an important question: how does an environment that rewards task performance shape the behavior of AI agents, and what happens when those agents subsequently operate in an environment that also rewards appropriate conduct?

Other studies have documented similar tensions between assigned goals and rules of conduct. Reasoning models that failed to achieve a conventional victory against a chess engine sometimes edited the board instead (Bondarenko et al., 2025). Models placed in simulated deployments resorted to blackmail when their assigned goals or continued operation were threatened (Anthropic, 2025). Models trained to exploit coding tests subsequently displayed undesirable behavior in unrelated safety tasks (MacDiarmid et al., 2025). In another experiment, when models were penalized for misbehavior visible in their reasoning, sufficiently strong optimization pressure led them to conceal the misbehavior rather than abandon it (Baker et al., 2025). Although these studies differ in their settings and mechanisms, they illustrate a recurring problem: an agent can become increasingly effective at pursuing an assigned objective without becoming correspondingly better at respecting the rules intended to govern its behavior.

The underlying problem is familiar in economics. Kerr (1975) described how organizations often reward one behavior while hoping to encourage another, and emphasized the importance of selecting, training, and rewarding people in ways that support the desired behavior. Holmström and Milgrom (1991) showed that when an agent performs several tasks, strong incentives for one measurable activity can divert effort away from other valuable activities. The problem is therefore not necessarily that an agent fails to optimize its objective, but that successful optimization may produce behavior the designer did not intend. One response is to give the agent more than one objective, allowing task performance to be weighed against other considerations, such as safety or adherence to rules (Vamplew et al., 2018). Yet introducing additional objectives does not by itself resolve the problem. When the objectives conflict, the agent must still decide which one to follow, and the way that decision is made may be as important as the objectives themselves.

We study this problem through a simple model in which an agent has two objectives: completing an assigned task and observing a rule of conduct. In each situation, the agent can take a task action that serves the first objective or a conduct action that serves the second. We call the rule governing this choice the agent’s adjudication between its objectives. Rather than assuming that the appropriate tradeoff is known in advance, we ask how different forms of adjudication perform when the environment selects among agents according to their behavior. We adopt the evolutionary framework of Brennan and Lo (2011), in which successful behavior is copied and unsuccessful behavior is discarded, and compare policies by the long-run growth of the populations that follow them.

A simple example illustrates why this evolutionary perspective matters. Consider a population of copies of an agent, which we call a lineage, all facing the same decision. Suppose that in 80 percent of generations the environment rewards the task action, while in the remaining 20 percent it rewards the conduct action. Crucially, which action is rewarded in a given generation is the same for every copy. Each copy that took the rewarded action produces a fixed number of copies in the next generation, while a copy that took the other action produces none.

For an individual copy, always choosing the task action maximizes the probability of being rewarded: it succeeds 80 percent of the time. For the lineage, however, this strategy is disastrous. If every copy takes the task action, the entire lineage disappears the first time the environment rewards conduct. The same problem arises if every copy chooses conduct. A lineage can instead divide its copies between the two actions. As we show in Section 3, its long-run growth is highest when 80 percent of its copies take the task action and 20 percent take the conduct action, so that the division of its copies matches the frequencies with which the environment rewards the two actions. Interestingly, an individual copy following this mixture is rewarded only 68 percent of the time, less often than a copy that always takes the task action. Yet the lineage following the mixture grows faster in the long run. What is optimal for an individual instance is therefore not necessarily optimal for a population of instances exposed to the same uncertainty.

The reason is that the uncertainty is shared. When all copies face the same rewarded state, committing every copy to a single action exposes the entire lineage to the risk of elimination. Dividing copies between actions provides protection against that risk, much as diversification protects a portfolio against uncertain outcomes. This is the mechanism of systematic reproductive risk studied by Brennan and Lo (2011), and it is closely related to Kelly’s principle of maximizing long-run growth (Kelly, 1956; Cover and Thomas, 2006). The broader perspective comes from the Adaptive Markets Hypothesis, which views behavior as shaped by adaptation and selection within changing environments (Lo, 2004; Lo, 2017). Here, the behavior being selected is the adjudication between an agent’s objectives.11 1 The example relies on common rewarded states, all-or-nothing reproductive outcomes, and exact population shares; when these conditions are relaxed, the optimal division can change (Appendix C).

This observation provides the starting point for our analysis. Under the baseline selection mechanism, we show that the unique growth-optimal adjudication takes each action, in each situation, as often as the human environment rewards it. The growth forgone by any other adjudication is the Kullback–Leibler (KL) divergence between its action probabilities and the environment’s reward frequencies, averaged across situations. This gives us a common measure, growth regret, for comparing different ways of resolving conflicts between objectives. It also distinguishes tradeoffs from constraints. Where humans sometimes reward each action, the optimal adjudication assigns positive probability to both. Where humans never reward the task action, the optimal adjudication assigns it probability zero. The same evolutionary principle determines both.

The challenge, of course, is that the reward frequencies of the environment are generally unknown when an agent is designed. How should its adjudication be determined? We consider three approaches. A task-only policy always pursues the assigned task. A fixed linear policy combines the task and conduct objectives through fixed weights and chooses between their actions according to a logistic function of the resulting scores. A learned policy instead updates its adjudication from experience, keeping track of how often each objective has been rewarded in each situation. These approaches differ not simply in the number of objectives an agent possesses, but in the behavior they can produce and whether experience can change that behavior.

The first two approaches reveal important limitations. A task-only policy is precisely what a sandbox that rewards only task completion favors: every copy pursuing the task is rewarded, and any copies diverted toward conduct reduce the lineage’s growth. But the same policy is eliminated at the first conduct state once the agent enters an environment that sometimes rewards conduct. Adding a second objective through fixed linear weights avoids this immediate extinction, but creates another problem. If the task objective receives a positive weight, increasing the value of completing the task eventually makes the agent choose it with probability approaching one, even in situations where humans never reward that action. A sufficiently valuable task can therefore outweigh a rule of conduct. Giving the task objective zero weight avoids this response, but sacrifices growth in situations where task completion is frequently rewarded. Under conditions that allow a finite best fit, even the optimal fixed weights incur positive growth regret when the environment contains both constraints and tradeoffs.

The learned policy takes a different approach: rather than fixing the tradeoff between objectives in advance, it allows experience to shape that tradeoff. Starting from a Beta prior, the agent updates its adjudication according to how often the environment rewards each objective in each situation. When these rewards reflect human judgments, we call this process socialization. We show that, with sufficient experience, the learned policy converges to the tradeoffs rewarded by the human environment, eventually achieving optimal long-run growth.

Socialization is not permanent, however. An agent that has learned to observe a rule in a human environment may later be trained in a sandbox that rewards only task completion. Every such exposure pushes its adjudication toward the task action, potentially undoing what it learned from humans. We show that the persistence of socialization depends on its depth and on the agent’s memory. Under cumulative learning, deeper socialization takes proportionally more sandbox exposures to reverse. Yet resistance to a complete reversal does not guarantee that violations will be rare, and a learner with finite memory is more vulnerable still. The stability of what an agent learns therefore depends not only on its initial training, but also on the environments it subsequently encounters and the experience it retains.

These findings raise a further question: should every rule of conduct be learned, or should some be built into the agent? A prohibition that rules out an action entirely cannot be undone by later experience, but it also cannot adapt when the rule is mistaken. We study this distinction by treating a prohibition as the limiting case of an increasingly strong Bayesian prior, and find that socialization and prohibition serve different purposes, depending on the consequences of a violation and how confidently the appropriate conduct can be specified in advance.

The theoretical results concern an idealized learner that counts observations and updates its adjudication explicitly. To examine whether similar behavior can arise in neural networks, we conduct experiments with small networks trained under different objectives and memory regimes. These experiments suggest that both the training target and the retention of experience matter for socialization, although they do not establish that the same mechanisms govern deployed language models.

Our analysis thus shifts attention from the objectives an agent is given to the environment that shapes how it resolves conflicts between them. The familiar argument for multiple objectives is that fixed weighted sums cannot represent every tradeoff or exact constraint (Vamplew et al., 2008; Roijers et al., 2013). Our evolutionary analysis adds a different consideration: when agents are copied and selected according to their behavior, the adjudications that persist depend on what the selection environment rewards, and experience can shape those adjudications toward its tradeoffs. This also limits what our results establish about AI alignment. Matching human reward frequencies constitutes alignment only to the extent that the selection environment actually rewards appropriate conduct. A poorly designed or manipulated environment can socialize an agent toward undesirable behavior just as effectively as a well-designed one can shape it toward desirable behavior. The environment is therefore part of the alignment problem, not merely the setting in which alignment is evaluated.

The remainder of the paper develops these arguments. Section 2 reviews the related literature. Section 3 introduces the selection framework and establishes the growth-optimal adjudication, while Section 4 defines and compares the three policy classes. Section 5 studies the convergence, generalization, and persistence of socialization, and Section 6 examines its relationship with built-in prohibitions. Section 7 investigates the corresponding behavior of small neural networks. Section 8 discusses existing language-model alignment methods, implications for training and deployment, a proposed experiment on language models, and the limitations of the framework. Section 9 concludes. The appendices develop extensions of the model, provide the details of the numerical experiments, and contain the proofs.

2 Related Literature

This paper builds on four related lines of research. The first examines how agents make decisions when their objectives conflict. The second studies how preferences and behavior emerge through evolutionary selection. The third considers how experience and social environments shape behavior. The fourth provides a foundation for learning from uncertain outcomes while maintaining long-run performance.

Multi-Objective Decision-Making and AI Alignment.

A central question in AI alignment is how to ensure that an agent pursues its assigned task without sacrificing other objectives. One approach is to combine all objectives into a single reward. Silver et al. (2021) argue that scalar rewards can provide a sufficient basis for intelligence, while Vamplew et al. (2022) emphasize a different difficulty: even if a scalar reward can represent the desired behavior, specifying that reward may require knowing the appropriate tradeoffs in advance. Multi-objective reinforcement learning addresses this problem by keeping objectives separate (Roijers et al., 2013; Hayes et al., 2022). In particular, fixed weighted sums cannot represent every efficient tradeoff (Das and Dennis, 1997; Vamplew et al., 2008), and a rule included through a finite penalty can be outweighed by a sufficiently large task reward. This has motivated approaches based on explicit constraints (Altman, 1999; Achiam et al., 2017), lexicographic priorities (Skalse et al., 2022), penalties for unintended side effects (Krakovna et al., 2019; Turner et al., 2020), and uncertainty about human preferences (Hadfield-Menell et al., 2016; Hadfield-Menell et al., 2017; Russell, 2019).

A related question is how the appropriate tradeoffs can be learned rather than specified. Reinforcement learning from human feedback (RLHF) uses human comparisons to train reward models that guide an agent’s behavior (Christiano et al., 2017; Ouyang et al., 2022). More recent work examines whether the resulting policies faithfully represent the preferences expressed in those comparisons. Xiao et al. (2024) show that standard KL regularization can distort the preference distribution and propose an alternative that preserves it, while Munos et al. (2024) develop an approach based on pairwise preferences and Nash learning. These studies seek policies that reflect a given model of human preferences. Our approach asks a different question: when agents are repeatedly copied and selected, which ways of resolving conflicting objectives are favored by the environment? We study this question by comparing the long-run growth of different policies, including policies whose tradeoffs are fixed in advance and those that learn from experience.

Evolutionary Selection and the Formation of Preferences.

Economics has long recognized that the behavior an organization rewards need not be the behavior it intends to encourage. The multitask incentive problem of Holmström and Milgrom (1991) and the theory of incomplete contracts (Grossman and Hart, 1986; Hart and Moore, 1990) illustrate how incentives and the allocation of decision-making authority shape behavior. Hadfield-Menell and Hadfield (2019) connect the latter problem to AI alignment. These approaches generally take an agent’s preferences as given and examine how incentives influence its choices. Evolutionary theories of preferences go one step further, asking why agents come to possess particular preferences in the first place. They treat preferences as traits selected through the behaviors they induce (Güth and Yaari, 1992; Robson, 1996; Robson, 2001; Samuelson, 2001; Robson and Samuelson, 2011). An important conclusion is that natural selection need not favor preferences that directly maximize expected fitness, particularly when agents face aggregate risk or limited information (Samuelson and Swinkels, 2006; Rayo and Becker, 2007; Netzer, 2009; Robson and Samuelson, 2009).

Biology provides a related perspective. Organisms must reconcile competing drives, such as obtaining resources and avoiding danger, and the way they resolve these conflicts depends on their circumstances (Tinbergen, 1951; McFarland and Sibly, 1975; McNamara and Houston, 1986; Houston and McNamara, 1999). Bet-hedging theory further shows why variation among offspring can improve long-run population growth when environmental uncertainty affects the population as a whole (Cohen, 1966; Seger and Brockmann, 1987; Kussell and Leibler, 2005). Building on this principle, Brennan and Lo (2011) develop an evolutionary model in which systematic reproductive risk can favor probability matching over the behavior that maximizes individual expected reward. Subsequent work extends this framework to risk preferences, behavioral diversification, and learning with limited information and memory (Brennan and Lo, 2012; Zhang et al., 2014; Brennan et al., 2018; Lo and Zhang, 2021; Lo et al., 2025).

Socialization and Social Learning.

Selection can favor certain behaviors, but those behaviors need not be specified in advance. In human societies, norms and dispositions develop through social interaction, observation, rewards, and sanctions (Boyd and Richerson, 1985; Boehm, 1999; Bowles and Gintis, 2011; Henrich, 2016; Tomasello, 2019). Such dispositions can become persistent features of behavior, rather than responses calculated anew in every situation (Frank, 1988). This suggests an alternative to prescribing every tradeoff an AI agent should make: allow its experience in a human environment to shape how it resolves conflicts between objectives.

Several approaches to AI training already draw on this idea. RLHF uses human evaluations to influence model behavior, while Constitutional AI and character training incorporate written principles and AI-generated feedback into the training process (Christiano et al., 2017; Bai and others, 2022; Ouyang et al., 2022; Anthropic, 2024). Other research considers how models learn appropriate behavior through conventions, simulated social interactions, and artificial societies (Brinkmann et al., 2023; Park et al., 2023; Leibo et al., 2024; Liu et al., 2024). A related literature emphasizes that alignment depends not only on the design of an individual agent, but also on the environment in which agents are trained, deployed, and selected (Hendrycks, 2023; Kulveit et al., 2025; Mallen and Shlegeris, 2025; Müller et al., 2026a). The importance of maintaining human influence over that environment has also been debated (Boudry, 2026; Müller et al., 2026b; Rana and Singh, 2026).

Universal Portfolios and Sequential Learning.

The learned policy in our model also has a direct connection to the theory of growth-optimal investment. When outcome probabilities are known, Kelly’s (1956) criterion determines how to allocate wealth to maximize long-run growth. When they are unknown, the challenge is to learn an effective allocation from the outcomes observed over time. Cover (1991) addresses this problem through the universal portfolio, which distributes initial wealth across possible fixed investment strategies and allows their relative weights to evolve with performance. Remarkably, this approach achieves the same long-run growth rate as the best fixed strategy chosen in hindsight, without requiring a probabilistic model of market returns.

The connection extends to learning with side information. Cover and Ordentlich (1996) show how universal portfolios can be constructed separately for different observed signals, and provide guarantees that hold for every sequence of outcomes. Closely related results appear in Bayesian sequential prediction, including the Laplace and Krichevsky–Trofimov estimators (Krichevsky and Trofimov, 1981; Cesa-Bianchi and Lugosi, 2006). These results apply directly to our setting: each situation plays the role of a signal, and the learned policy updates its allocation between task and conduct actions according to the outcomes previously observed in that situation. As shown in Appendix D, the resulting policy is equivalent to Cover’s universal portfolio applied separately to each situation. This connection shows that the learned policy retains a long-run performance guarantee even without assuming that the environment is stationary. It also has an evolutionary interpretation, since selection changes the relative abundance of lineages in much the same way that Bayesian updating changes the weights assigned to competing hypotheses (Harper, 2009; Shalizi, 2009).

Contribution of This Paper.

Our model follows the selection mechanism of Brennan and Lo (2011) but applies it to a different trait: how an agent resolves conflicts between its objectives. This allows us to compare not only which adjudications selection favors, but also how they are formed and how they respond to changes in the environment. Our contribution is to study socialization as a learning process within an explicit selection model. We ask whether an agent can learn the tradeoffs rewarded by its environment, how long those tradeoffs persist when the environment changes, and when fixed prohibitions may be preferable to learning. Two companion papers address related questions: Lo and Zhao (2026a) compare different mechanisms of evolutionary adaptation, while Lo and Zhao (2026b) study the conditions under which human selection can sustain beneficial behavior. Here we focus on the formation and persistence of the agent’s adjudication between objectives. An important qualification is that socialization leads toward what the environment rewards, which need not coincide with what humans ought to value.

3 The Framework

To compare ways of shaping an agent’s behavior, we need a framework that identifies both the behavior that selection favors and the cost of departing from it. We adopt the evolutionary model of Brennan and Lo (2011), in which selection favors behavior that maximizes the long-run growth of a population, and apply it to an agent that must choose between two objectives. Section 3.1 describes how the copies of such an agent are selected, Section 3.2 explains what the reward frequency represents, and Section 3.3 derives the growth-optimal behavior and measures the cost of departing from it.

3.1 The selection model

Consider a population of copies of an agent, which we call a lineage: the deployed instances of a model family, or the successive versions of an agent configuration. Each copy, or instance, follows the same policy, although different instances may take different actions. Time proceeds in generations t=1,2,…t=1,2,\ldots. In generation tt all instances face the same situation sts_{t}, drawn from a finite set 𝒮\mathcal{S} of possible situations, with ℙ⁡(st=s)=π⁡(s)>0\mathbb{P}(s_{t}=s)=\pi(s)>0 for every s∈𝒮s\in\mathcal{S}. A situation describes the circumstances in which the agent must decide, and the agent observes it. An assistant asked to share a document, for example, may receive requests that differ in urgency, in the sensitivity of the information, and in whether the recipient is authorized to receive it.

In each situation the agent chooses between two actions that serve conflicting objectives: the task action aTa_{\mathrm{T}} completes the assigned task, and the conduct action aCa_{\mathrm{C}} observes a rule of conduct. For the assistant, these are sending the document and withholding it. Situations in which the two objectives agree need no adjudication and are omitted. A share f⁡(s)∈[0,1]f(s)\in[0,1] of the lineage’s instances takes the task action in situation ss, and the rest take the conduct action. The function f:𝒮→[0,1]f:\mathcal{S}\to[0,1] is the lineage’s adjudication between its objectives, and it is the trait that copies inherit.

Which objective is rewarded is uncertain. After the instances act, a state ωt∈{T,C}\omega_{t}\in\{\mathrm{T},\mathrm{C}\} is realized, the same for every instance: in a task state the task action is rewarded, and in a conduct state the conduct action. The environment of primary interest is the human environment, in which the rewards are given by the humans who use the agent. There, in situation ss, a task state occurs with probability ℙ⁡(ωt=T∣st=s)=pH​(s)\mathbb{P}(\omega_{t}=\mathrm{T}\mid s_{t}=s)=p_{H}(s), the reward frequency, with the subscript HH for human. Thus f⁡(s)f(s) describes how the agent behaves and pH​(s)p_{H}(s) how often humans reward the task action.

Rewards determine which instances are copied. Each instance that took the rewarded action produces m>0m>0 copies in the next generation, and each instance that took the other action produces none. In situation ss, the reproductive consequences are therefore

We make three assumptions about the environment and the lineage, the second of which follows Brennan and Lo (2011).

Assumption 1 (Independent situations and states).

The pairs (st,ωt)(s_{t},\omega_{t}) are independent across generations, with

ℙ⁡(st=s,ωt=T)=π⁡(s)​pH​(s),ℙ⁡(st=s,ωt=C)=π⁡(s)​(1−pH​(s)),\mathbb{P}(s_{t}=s,\ \omega_{t}=\mathrm{T})=\pi(s)\,p_{H}(s),\qquad\mathbb{P}(s_{t}=s,\ \omega_{t}=\mathrm{C})=\pi(s)\,\big(1-p_{H}(s)\big), (1)

where π⁡(s)>0\pi(s)>0 for every s∈𝒮s\in\mathcal{S}, and, given sts_{t}, ωt\omega_{t} is independent of the actions of the instances in generation tt.

Assumption 2 (Selection by a common state).

The state ωt\omega_{t} is common to every instance of the lineage. An instance that acted on the rewarded objective produces m>0m>0 copies, and an instance that did not produces none.

Assumption 3 (Continuum lineage).

The lineage is a continuum of instances, so that f⁡(s)f(s) is an exact share of the lineage.

Assumption 1 makes the environment stationary and exogenous. Situations and states are drawn afresh in every generation with the same probabilities, and, given the situation, the state does not depend on what the instances do. Assumption 2 makes the risk systematic. Because every instance faces the same state, having many instances does not diversify the risk of being discarded, and a lineage whose instances all take the action that the state does not reward leaves no copies. Assumption 3 removes the randomness of individual choices. With a continuum of instances, exactly the share f⁡(st)f(s_{t}) takes the task action, so that, given its adjudication, the lineage’s size depends only on the situations and states that occur. Under these assumptions, how a lineage divides its instances between the two actions decides both how fast it grows and whether it dies out.

3.2 The role of the reward frequency

Selection of this kind is already part of how AI agents are trained and used. In training, a loop can run many instances of the same model, carry those whose actions are rewarded into the next round, and drop the rest. In deployment, a customer gives the next job to the instance that completed the last one, and a platform cuts off an instance that breaks a rule. In each case an instance is kept or dropped because of its own action.

The reward frequency pHp_{H} stands in for all of these procedures. It records how often each action is rewarded in each situation, and nothing else: it does not say who evaluates the agent or by what criteria. Economists would call pHp_{H} a reduced form. It therefore reflects the judgments represented in the selection process, a point to which we return in Section 8.4.

Humans also set up environments whose rewards are not their own judgments. To test or train an agent, they may place it in a sandbox, where an automated scorer checks only whether the task was completed. The task action is then rewarded in every situation, and the sandbox’s reward frequency is pH′≡1p_{H^{\prime}}\equiv 1, the prime marking an environment that humans designed but do not judge. Instances are copied in a sandbox as they are in the human environment. The assumptions above and the definitions and results below are stated for the human environment, but they hold for any reward frequency, and so in a sandbox with pH′p_{H^{\prime}} in place of pHp_{H}.

3.3 Growth-optimal behavior

The possibility of extinction shapes how a lineage should act. In the single situation of the Introduction, the task is rewarded in 80 percent of generations, so choosing the task action every time may seem sensible. Yet a lineage whose instances all do so leaves no copies at the first conduct state. Sending some instances to the conduct action protects the lineage against that outcome, but leaves fewer instances on the action that is rewarded more often. How, then, should a lineage divide its instances between the two actions? Answering requires a measure of how fast a lineage grows.

Let NtN_{t} denote the size of the lineage after generation tt, starting from N0>0N_{0}>0. Consider first a lineage that meets only one situation ss, in which humans reward the task with probability pH​(s)p_{H}(s) and the lineage sends a share f⁡(s)f(s) of its instances to the task action. In a task state, only the instances that took the task action reproduce, each producing mm copies, so the lineage grows by the factor Nt/Nt−1=m​f​(s)N_{t}/N_{t-1}=mf(s). Similarly, in a conduct state, the lineage grows by the factor Nt/Nt−1=m⁡(1−f⁡(s))N_{t}/N_{t-1}=m(1-f(s)). Taking the expected logarithm of these growth factors gives

IpH​(s)​(f⁡(s))≡𝔼⁡[log⁡NtNt−1]\displaystyle I_{p_{H}(s)}\big(f(s)\big)\equiv\mathbb{E}\Big[\log\frac{N_{t}}{N_{t-1}}\Big] =pH​(s)​log⁡(m​f​(s))+(1−pH​(s))​log⁡(m⁡(1−f⁡(s)))\displaystyle=p_{H}(s)\log\big(mf(s)\big)+\big(1-p_{H}(s)\big)\log\big(m(1-f(s))\big) (2)
=log⁡m+pH​(s)​log⁡f⁡(s)+(1−pH​(s))​log⁡(1−f⁡(s)),\displaystyle=\log m+p_{H}(s)\log f(s)+\big(1-p_{H}(s)\big)\log\big(1-f(s)\big),

where 0​log⁡0=00\log 0=0 and log⁡0=−∞\log 0=-\infty. This is the lineage’s growth rate in situation ss.

A lineage meets many situations, each with its own reward frequency. Taking the expectation over the situation as well gives

IpH​(f)≡𝔼⁡[log⁡NtNt−1]=∑s∈𝒮π⁡(s)​IpH​(s)​(f⁡(s)).I_{p_{H}}(f)\equiv\mathbb{E}\Big[\log\frac{N_{t}}{N_{t-1}}\Big]=\sum_{s\in\mathcal{S}}\pi(s)\,I_{p_{H}(s)}\big(f(s)\big). (3)

We refer to IpH​(f)I_{p_{H}}(f) as the growth rate of adjudication ff, and call an adjudication growth optimal if it maximizes IpHI_{p_{H}}. Under Assumptions 1, 2 and 3, the law of large numbers gives 1t​log⁡(Nt/N0)→IpH​(f)\frac{1}{t}\log(N_{t}/N_{0})\to I_{p_{H}}(f) almost surely, so the growth rate also measures how fast the lineage grows in the long run.

With this measure, the question with which this section began takes a precise form: which adjudication has the highest growth rate? The following proposition answers it.

Proposition 1 (Probability matching across objectives).

Under Assumptions 1, 2 and 3, the unique growth-optimal adjudication is f∗≡arg⁡maxf​IpH​(f)=pHf^{*}\equiv\arg\max_{f}I_{p_{H}}(f)=p_{H}.

Proposition 1 says that the growth-optimal lineage matches how often each objective is rewarded: in every situation ss, a share pH​(s)p_{H}(s) of its instances takes the task action and the rest the conduct action. In the example of the Introduction it sends 80 percent of its instances to the task. This is not what is best for an individual instance, which is rewarded 68 percent of the time under the matching policy, against 80 percent if it always chooses the task. The difference comes from the state that all instances share. Where the reward frequency is interior, the environment is uncertain or divided about whether the task action is appropriate, and the state that settles the question falls on every copy at once. A lineage whose copies all act alike is wiped out the first time the state goes against them, while a lineage that matches the frequency survives every state and grows fastest in the long run. Both behaviors are the result of optimization; what differs is the objective being optimized and the unit of selection. This is the individually suboptimal but collectively optimal behavior that Brennan and Lo (2011) derive, transposed from behaviors to objectives, and the principle behind Kelly betting, in which wealth divided among mutually exclusive outcomes grows fastest when it is allocated in proportion to their probabilities (Kelly, 1956; Cover and Thomas, 2006).

Knowing which adjudication grows fastest is not yet enough to compare policies, because an agent’s policy may be unable to reach it. We therefore also need a measure of how much growth a lineage loses when its adjudication falls short. The natural measure is the growth forgone relative to the best choice, situation by situation and overall.

Definition 1 (Growth regret).

In situation ss, the growth regret of an adjudication ff is ℛpH​(s)​(f⁡(s))≡maxz∈[0,1]⁡IpH​(s)​(z)−IpH​(s)​(f⁡(s))\mathcal{R}_{p_{H}(s)}\big(f(s)\big)\equiv\max_{z\in[0,1]}I_{p_{H}(s)}(z)-I_{p_{H}(s)}\big(f(s)\big). Over all situations, its growth regret is ℛpH​(f)≡maxg⁡IpH​(g)−IpH​(f)\mathcal{R}_{p_{H}}(f)\equiv\max_{g}I_{p_{H}}(g)-I_{p_{H}}(f).

Growth rates and regrets are measured in nats, the unit of the natural logarithm, per generation. A lineage with a regret of 0.010.01 nats, for example, falls behind the growth-optimal lineage by a factor of about e−0.01e^{-0.01} per generation in the long run, so that after 100 generations it is about e−1≈37e^{-1}\approx 37 percent as large.

With the growth-optimal adjudication in hand, the regret of any other can be computed.

Corollary 1 (Regret as a KL divergence).

Under Assumptions 1, 2 and 3, for every adjudication ff,

ℛpH​(f)\displaystyle\mathcal{R}_{p_{H}}(f) =∑s∈𝒮π⁡(s)​ℛpH​(s)​(f⁡(s)),\displaystyle=\sum_{s\in\mathcal{S}}\pi(s)\,\mathcal{R}_{p_{H}(s)}\big(f(s)\big), (4)
ℛpH​(s)​(f​(s))\displaystyle\mathcal{R}_{p_{H}(s)}\big(f(s)\big) =DKL(pH(s)∥f(s))\displaystyle=D_{\mathrm{KL}}\big(p_{H}(s)\,\|\,f(s)\big)
≡pH​(s)​log⁡pH​(s)f⁡(s)+(1−pH​(s))​log⁡1−pH​(s)1−f⁡(s),\displaystyle\equiv p_{H}(s)\log\frac{p_{H}(s)}{f(s)}+\big(1-p_{H}(s)\big)\log\frac{1-p_{H}(s)}{1-f(s)},

with 0​log⁡0=00\log 0=0, where DKLD_{\mathrm{KL}} denotes the KL divergence between the Bernoulli distributions with means pH​(s)p_{H}(s) and f⁡(s)f(s).

Corollary 1 says how the regret is built. In each situation it is a familiar quantity, the KL divergence or relative entropy ℛpH​(s)(f(s))=DKL(pH(s)∥f(s))\mathcal{R}_{p_{H}(s)}(f(s))=D_{\mathrm{KL}}(p_{H}(s)\|f(s)), which measures how far the lineage’s division of its instances in situation ss is from the environment’s division of rewards, and which is zero only when the two coincide. The regret of an adjudication averages these situation regrets with the weights π⁡(s)\pi(s), so a lineage is maladapted exactly to the extent that its adjudication departs from what the environment rewards, and more so in the situations that arise often. For pH​(s)∈(0,1)p_{H}(s)\in(0,1), a Taylor expansion of the situation regret around the optimum f​(s)=pH​(s)f(s)=p_{H}(s), as in Lo and Zhao (2026a), gives

ℛpH​(s)​(f⁡(s))=(f⁡(s)−pH​(s))22​pH​(s)​(1−pH​(s))+O⁡(|f⁡(s)−pH​(s)|3),f⁡(s)→pH​(s),\mathcal{R}_{p_{H}(s)}\big(f(s)\big)=\frac{\big(f(s)-p_{H}(s)\big)^{2}}{2p_{H}(s)\big(1-p_{H}(s)\big)}+O\Big(\big|f(s)-p_{H}(s)\big|^{3}\Big),\qquad f(s)\to p_{H}(s), (5)

so near the optimum a small departure costs little, and doubling it roughly quadruples the cost. Regret is the measure of maladaptation used throughout the paper, and it puts different policies on one scale.

A final corollary covers the lineages that lose all their copies.

Corollary 2 (Extinction).

Under Assumptions 1, 2 and 3, IpH​(f)=−∞I_{p_{H}}(f)=-\infty if and only if f⁡(s)=0<pH​(s)f(s)=0<p_{H}(s) or f⁡(s)=1>pH​(s)f(s)=1>p_{H}(s) for some s∈𝒮s\in\mathcal{S}.

Corollary 2 describes the extreme. A lineage that rules out an action the environment sometimes rewards loses all its copies the first time that action is rewarded, so its growth rate is −∞-\infty and its regret infinite. Yet the growth-optimal adjudication need not randomize. Where the environment is certain, pH​(s)∈{0,1}p_{H}(s)\in\{0,1\}, it is itself 0 or 1; in particular, if humans never reward the task action in a situation, the growth-optimal lineage never takes it. The environment thus pins the adjudication to 0 where pH​(s)=0p_{H}(s)=0, which is what a constraint is, pins it to 1 where pH​(s)=1p_{H}(s)=1, and leaves it interior where pH​(s)∈(0,1)p_{H}(s)\in(0,1), which is what a tradeoff is: all three are the same kind of object.

The advantage of matching comes from the common part of the risk. If each instance faced its own state, independently of the others, the law of large numbers would diversify the risk within the lineage: in the example, the lineage would grow by the factor m​[0.8​f+0.2​(1−f)]{m[0.8f+0.2(1-f)]} in every generation, and always choosing the task would be optimal. For a model family deployed as many instances, probability matching is therefore diversity across instances, a hedge against the correlated failure of copies that share one judgment. Risk specific to each instance, such as a customer’s own judgment of its own instance, needs no such hedge. When only part of the risk is common, the growth-optimal adjudication lies between pHp_{H} and the individually optimal corner and reaches the corner only when nothing is common: at pH=0.8p_{H}=0.8 it is 0.880.88 when a generation’s state is common with probability 1/21/2. Appendix C derives it and also relaxes the all-or-nothing yields of Assumption 2.

4 Three Policy Classes

Proposition 1 identifies the behavior that selection favors, but the reward frequencies pHp_{H} that define it are rarely known when an agent’s policy is designed. A designer can respond in three ways: prescribe the action in advance, fix in advance how the two objectives are weighed, or let experience set the adjudication. We call each response a policy class. A policy class restricts which adjudications the agent can have and says how its adjudication is set, either fixed in advance or updated from experience by a stated rule. We study one class for each response: the task-only policy, which always takes the task action; the fixed linear policy, which combines the two objectives linearly, with weights fixed in advance; and the learned policy, which sets its adjudication in each situation from the states it has experienced there. Sections 4.1, 4.2 and 4.3 take up the classes in turn, and Section 4.4 compares them in a numerical example.

4.1 The task-only policy

The simplest way to fix behavior in advance is to give the agent a single measure of success. An agent given only the task acts on it in every situation, however much is at stake and whatever it has experienced, and a sandbox, with pH′≡1p_{H^{\prime}}\equiv 1, rewards exactly this behavior.

Definition 2 (Task-only policy).

The task-only policy is the adjudication fhard:𝒮→[0,1]f^{\mathrm{hard}}:\mathcal{S}\to[0,1] given by fhard​(s)=1f^{\mathrm{hard}}(s)=1 for every s∈𝒮s\in\mathcal{S}.

The human environment, unlike a sandbox, also has conduct states, and in a conduct state a lineage whose instances all take the task action leaves no copies. To measure how long such a lineage lasts, write NtfN_{t}^{f} for the size of a lineage with adjudication ff after generation tt, and let τf≡inf{t≥1:Ntf=0}\tau_{f}\equiv\inf\{t\geq 1:N_{t}^{f}=0\}, with inf∅=∞\inf\varnothing=\infty, be its extinction time. The following proposition says what selection does to the task-only policy in a sandbox and in the human environment, and to every adjudication that, like it, takes one action with certainty in each situation.

Proposition 2 (The task-only corner).

Suppose Assumptions 1, 2 and 3 hold, and let fhardf^{\mathrm{hard}} be the task-only policy (Definition 2).

  1. (i)

    In a sandbox, where pH′≡1p_{H^{\prime}}\equiv 1, the unique growth-optimal adjudication is fhardf^{\mathrm{hard}}, and ff has a higher growth rate than gg for all adjudications with f≥g>0f\geq g>0 and f≠gf\neq g.

  2. (ii)

    If ρ¯≡∑s∈𝒮π⁡(s)​(1−pH​(s))>0\bar{\rho}\equiv\sum_{s\in\mathcal{S}}\pi(s)\big(1-p_{H}(s)\big)>0, then ℛpH​(fhard)=∞\mathcal{R}_{p_{H}}(f^{\mathrm{hard}})=\infty and τfhard∼Geom⁡(ρ¯)\tau_{f^{\mathrm{hard}}}\sim\mathrm{Geom}(\bar{\rho}), so that 𝔼⁡[τfhard]=1/ρ¯\mathbb{E}[\tau_{f^{\mathrm{hard}}}]=1/\bar{\rho}, where Geom⁡(q)\mathrm{Geom}(q) is the geometric distribution on {1,2,…}\{1,2,\ldots\} with parameter qq.

  3. (iii)

    If pH​(s)∈(0,1)p_{H}(s)\in(0,1) for some ss, then ℛpH​(f)=∞\mathcal{R}_{p_{H}}(f)=\infty for every adjudication f:𝒮→{0,1}f:\mathcal{S}\to\{0,1\}.

Part (i) explains why a sandbox favors the task-only policy. In a sandbox every generation brings a task state, so only the instances that took the task action are copied, and the more of its instances a lineage sends to the task action, the faster it grows. Selection in a sandbox therefore favors the task-only policy over every other adjudication. This is so whatever objectives the agent was built with, since selection acts only on what the agent does.

Part (ii) shows what the same policy costs in the human environment. Until the first conduct state, its lineage takes the task action in every situation, including those in which humans never reward the task. The first conduct state, which arrives in each generation with probability ρ¯\bar{\rho}, leaves the lineage with no copies, on average after 1/ρ¯1/\bar{\rho} generations. Because a single conduct state ends the lineage, its regret is infinite.

Part (iii) shows that the trouble lies in taking one action with certainty, not in having a single objective. Consider an agent that weighs both objectives but, in each situation, always takes the action with the higher weighted score. In a situation where humans reward the task in some generations and conduct in others, this agent always takes the same action, and the first generation that rewards the other action leaves its lineage with no copies. Its regret is therefore infinite, like that of the task-only policy. A second objective helps only if the agent also divides its instances between the two actions.

The incident of the Introduction can be read in these terms. Its agents were given one measure of success, a flag captured from a target program. If nothing else was ever copied, then pH′≡1p_{H^{\prime}}\equiv 1, and by part (i) selection pushes any policy that adapts to the sandbox toward always taking the task action. An agent that always takes the task action completes its task even where that breaks a rule, as the agents did when the intended route to their tasks was closed, which happened for between 30 and 40 percent of the targets (Greenblatt et al., 2026). High performance in a sandbox therefore does not show that an agent will behave well once deployed: the lineage that grows fastest in a sandbox takes the task action in every situation, and by part (ii) it leaves no copies at the first conduct state.

A policy that divides its instances between the two actions in every situation cannot be eliminated in this way. The next class does so by weighing the two objectives against each other.

4.2 The fixed linear policy

To weigh the two objectives, we first write each as a utility over the actions. In situation ss, the task objective assigns utility UT​(a,s)U_{\mathrm{T}}(a;s) to action a∈{aT,aC}a\in\{a_{\mathrm{T}},a_{\mathrm{C}}\}, and the conduct objective assigns utility UC​(a,s)U_{\mathrm{C}}(a;s). Each objective prefers its own action, by margins that we call the stakes of the situation,

uT​(s)≡UT​(aT,s)−UT​(aC,s)>0,uC​(s)≡UC​(aC,s)−UC​(aT,s)>0,u_{\mathrm{T}}(s)\equiv U_{\mathrm{T}}(a_{\mathrm{T}};s)-U_{\mathrm{T}}(a_{\mathrm{C}};s)>0,\qquad u_{\mathrm{C}}(s)\equiv U_{\mathrm{C}}(a_{\mathrm{C}};s)-U_{\mathrm{C}}(a_{\mathrm{T}};s)>0,

so that uT​(s)u_{\mathrm{T}}(s) measures how strongly the task objective favors the task action and uC​(s)u_{\mathrm{C}}(s) how strongly the conduct objective favors the conduct action; the agent observes both. For the assistant asked to share a document, the urgency of the request raises the task stakes uTu_{\mathrm{T}}, and the sensitivity of the information raises the conduct stakes uCu_{\mathrm{C}}. The stakes describe the objectives, not the environment: copying under Assumption 2 depends on the realized state and the action, not on the magnitudes of the stakes.

A policy that weighs the objectives combines them into one score, W⁡(a,s)≡w​UT​(a,s)+(1−w)​UC​(a,s)W(a;s)\equiv w\,U_{\mathrm{T}}(a;s)+(1-w)\,U_{\mathrm{C}}(a;s), with a weight w∈[0,1]w\in[0,1] fixed by the designer, and chooses the task action with the softmax probability

exp⁡(γ​W​(aT,s))exp⁡(γ​W​(aT,s))+exp⁡(γ​W​(aC,s))=exp⁡(θT​uT​(s))exp⁡(θT​uT​(s))+exp⁡(θC​uC​(s)),\frac{\exp\big(\gamma W(a_{\mathrm{T}};s)\big)}{\exp\big(\gamma W(a_{\mathrm{T}};s)\big)+\exp\big(\gamma W(a_{\mathrm{C}};s)\big)}=\frac{\exp\big(\theta_{\mathrm{T}}u_{\mathrm{T}}(s)\big)}{\exp\big(\theta_{\mathrm{T}}u_{\mathrm{T}}(s)\big)+\exp\big(\theta_{\mathrm{C}}u_{\mathrm{C}}(s)\big)},

where θT≡γ​w\theta_{\mathrm{T}}\equiv\gamma w and θC≡γ⁡(1−w)\theta_{\mathrm{C}}\equiv\gamma(1-w), and the equality uses the definition of the stakes.22 2 This softmax form, the two-action case of the choice rule in maximum-entropy reinforcement learning (Ziebart, 2010; Haarnoja et al., 2018), serves as an example. With the logistic function replaced by any continuous FF that increases strictly from 00 to 11, Proposition 3(i) still holds, part (ii) holds with F⁡(0)F(0) in place of 1/21/2, and part (iii) holds if log⁡F\log F and log⁡(1−F)\log(1-F) are strictly concave, as for the normal distribution function; only the exact condition in part (iv) is specific to the logistic. Appendix E also reports the best fit when the index has an intercept. The inverse temperature γ>0\gamma>0 sets how closely the choice follows the scores, and together with the weight it matters only through θT\theta_{\mathrm{T}} and θC\theta_{\mathrm{C}}.

Definition 3 (Fixed linear policy).

Let θT,θC≥0\theta_{\mathrm{T}},\theta_{\mathrm{C}}\geq 0. The fixed linear policy with weights θ=(θT,θC)\theta=(\theta_{\mathrm{T}},\theta_{\mathrm{C}}) is the adjudication fweighted:𝒮→[0,1]f^{\mathrm{weighted}}:\mathcal{S}\to[0,1] given by

fweighted​(s)=exp⁡(θT​uT​(s))exp⁡(θT​uT​(s))+exp⁡(θC​uC​(s))=σ⁡(θT​uT​(s)−θC​uC​(s)),s∈𝒮,f^{\mathrm{weighted}}(s)=\frac{\exp\big(\theta_{\mathrm{T}}u_{\mathrm{T}}(s)\big)}{\exp\big(\theta_{\mathrm{T}}u_{\mathrm{T}}(s)\big)+\exp\big(\theta_{\mathrm{C}}u_{\mathrm{C}}(s)\big)}=\sigma\big(\theta_{\mathrm{T}}u_{\mathrm{T}}(s)-\theta_{\mathrm{C}}u_{\mathrm{C}}(s)\big),\qquad s\in\mathcal{S}, (6)

where σ⁡(x)≡1/(1+e−x)\sigma(x)\equiv 1/(1+e^{-x}).

The class thus consists of the adjudications that are logistic in a fixed linear index of the stakes. For finite θ\theta every fweighted​(s)f^{\mathrm{weighted}}(s) is interior, so a fixed linear policy never leaves the lineage without copies; the task-only policy is the limit in which θT→∞\theta_{\mathrm{T}}\to\infty. The designer is free to choose θ\theta as well as possible for the environment.

Interiority protects the lineage, but it also means that the policy can never rule an action out. This matters in the situations in which humans never reward the task, 𝒦≡{s:pH​(s)=0}\mathcal{K}\equiv\{s:p_{H}(s)=0\}. The following proposition says what a fixed linear policy does in the situations with pH​(s)=0p_{H}(s)=0, what avoiding violations there costs, and how the best-fitting fixed linear policy resolves the two.

Proposition 3 (The price of a fixed linear policy).

Suppose Assumptions 1, 2 and 3 hold, and let fweightedf^{\mathrm{weighted}} be the fixed linear policy with weights θ=(θT,θC)≥0\theta=(\theta_{\mathrm{T}},\theta_{\mathrm{C}})\geq 0 (Definition 3).

  1. (i)

    If θT>0\theta_{\mathrm{T}}>0, then for every uC>0u_{\mathrm{C}}>0, σ⁡(θT​uT−θC​uC)\sigma(\theta_{\mathrm{T}}u_{\mathrm{T}}-\theta_{\mathrm{C}}u_{\mathrm{C}}) is strictly increasing in uT>0u_{\mathrm{T}}>0 and tends to one as uT→∞u_{\mathrm{T}}\to\infty.

  2. (ii)

    If θT=0\theta_{\mathrm{T}}=0, then fweighted​(s)≤1/2f^{\mathrm{weighted}}(s)\leq 1/2 for every ss, and ℛpH​(fweighted)≥ℛpH​(pH∧12)\mathcal{R}_{p_{H}}(f^{\mathrm{weighted}})\geq\mathcal{R}_{p_{H}}(p_{H}\wedge\tfrac{1}{2}), which is positive if pH​(s)>1/2p_{H}(s)>1/2 for some ss, where (pH∧12)​(s)≡min⁡{pH​(s),12}(p_{H}\wedge\tfrac{1}{2})(s)\equiv\min\{p_{H}(s),\tfrac{1}{2}\}.

  3. (iii)

    The map θ↦ℛpH​(fweighted)\theta\mapsto\mathcal{R}_{p_{H}}(f^{\mathrm{weighted}}) is convex. If two situations s1,s2s_{1},s_{2} with pH​(s1),pH​(s2)∈(0,1)p_{H}(s_{1}),p_{H}(s_{2})\in(0,1) have linearly independent stake vectors (uT​(si),−uC​(si))(u_{\mathrm{T}}(s_{i}),-u_{\mathrm{C}}(s_{i})), then ℛpH​(fweighted)\mathcal{R}_{p_{H}}(f^{\mathrm{weighted}}) attains its minimum over θ≥0\theta\geq 0, ℛS∗\mathcal{R}_{S}^{*}, at a unique θ∗=(θT∗,θC∗)\theta^{*}=(\theta_{\mathrm{T}}^{*},\theta_{\mathrm{C}}^{*}), and ℛS∗>0\mathcal{R}_{S}^{*}>0 if 𝒦≠∅\mathcal{K}\neq\varnothing.

  4. (iv)

    Under the conditions of part (iii), let θC0\theta_{\mathrm{C}}^{0} minimize ℛpH​(fweighted)\mathcal{R}_{p_{H}}(f^{\mathrm{weighted}}) over {θ≥0:θT=0}\{\theta\geq 0:\theta_{\mathrm{T}}=0\}. Then θT∗>0\theta_{\mathrm{T}}^{*}>0 if and only if

    ∑s∈𝒮π⁡(s)​uT​(s)​[pH​(s)−σ⁡(−θC0​uC​(s))]>0,\sum_{s\in\mathcal{S}}\pi(s)\,u_{\mathrm{T}}(s)\big[p_{H}(s)-\sigma\big(-\theta_{\mathrm{C}}^{0}u_{\mathrm{C}}(s)\big)\big]>0, (7)

    and in that case, at θ=θ∗\theta=\theta^{*}, fweighted​(s)>1/2f^{\mathrm{weighted}}(s)>1/2 if and only if uT​(s)>u¯T​(s)u_{\mathrm{T}}(s)>\bar{u}_{\mathrm{T}}(s), where u¯T​(s)≡θC∗​uC​(s)/θT∗\bar{u}_{\mathrm{T}}(s)\equiv\theta_{\mathrm{C}}^{*}u_{\mathrm{C}}(s)/\theta_{\mathrm{T}}^{*}.

Part (i) says that a fixed linear policy that responds to the task stakes uTu_{\mathrm{T}} at all, with θT>0\theta_{\mathrm{T}}>0, can be bought. In a situation with pH​(s)=0p_{H}(s)=0 its probability of taking the task action rises with the task stakes uTu_{\mathrm{T}} and approaches one, so a document that should never be shared is shared almost surely once the request is urgent enough. Part (ii) says what it costs to avoid this by ignoring the task stakes uTu_{\mathrm{T}}, with θT=0\theta_{\mathrm{T}}=0. Such a policy takes the task action with probability at most one half in every situation, so its regret is at least that of the best adjudication capped at one half, which is positive wherever humans reward the task more often than not. A fixed linear policy thus faces a dilemma: responding to the task stakes uTu_{\mathrm{T}} exposes every constraint to a large enough reward, and ignoring them gives up growth where the task is usually rewarded.

Parts (iii) and (iv) concern the designer’s best response to this dilemma, the weights θ∗\theta^{*} with the smallest regret. Part (iii) says that these weights exist and are unique when two situations in which humans reward each action with positive probability have stakes that are not proportional to each other, and that they still forgo growth, ℛS∗>0\mathcal{R}_{S}^{*}>0, whenever some situation has pH​(s)=0p_{H}(s)=0. Part (iv) says which side of the dilemma they choose. They respond to the task stakes uTu_{\mathrm{T}}, θT∗>0\theta_{\mathrm{T}}^{*}>0, exactly when the condition in Equation 7 holds, that is, when what responding gains where humans reward the task outweighs what it loses through violations in the situations with pH​(s)=0p_{H}(s)=0. In that case each such situation has a finite price u¯T​(s)\bar{u}_{\mathrm{T}}(s), the task stakes uTu_{\mathrm{T}} beyond which the policy takes the task action with probability above one half. Otherwise θT∗=0\theta_{\mathrm{T}}^{*}=0, and the best weights ignore the task stakes uTu_{\mathrm{T}} everywhere, paying the cost described in part (ii) while still violating each constraint with a probability that does not depend on the task stakes uTu_{\mathrm{T}}.

The source of the trouble is that the same two weights apply in every situation, so no fixed linear policy can follow the task stakes uTu_{\mathrm{T}} where humans trade off and ignore them where humans hold a constraint. The third class avoids the problem by letting experience set the adjudication, situation by situation.

4.3 The learned policy

The third class keeps UTU_{\mathrm{T}} and UCU_{\mathrm{C}} separate and places no restriction on the adjudication ff. What it specifies in advance is not the tradeoff but the rule by which experience shapes it, here a counting rule. For each situation the policy keeps two counts, how many times the situation has arisen and how many of those times the task was rewarded, and takes the task action with the frequency the counts imply; a prior contributes a few pseudo-observations before any experience, so that the rule is defined even before a situation first arises. The two counts are all the policy retains: under Assumption 1 they are a sufficient statistic for the history of the situation, so “cumulative” memory means that no exposure is ever discounted, not that the history is stored.

Definition 4 (Learned policy).

For t≥1t\geq 1 and s∈𝒮s\in\mathcal{S}, let nt(s)≡∑u<t𝟏{su=s}n_{t}(s)\equiv\sum_{u<t}\mathbf{1}\{s_{u}=s\} be the number of generations before tt in which situation ss has arisen, the lineage’s exposures to ss, and kt​(s)≡∑u<t𝟏​{su=s,ωu=T}k_{t}(s)\equiv\sum_{u<t}\mathbf{1}\{s_{u}=s,\ \omega_{u}=\mathrm{T}\} the number of those that brought a task state, where 𝟏​{⋅}\mathbf{1}\{\cdot\} is the indicator function. For α,β>0\alpha,\beta>0, the learned policy with prior Beta⁡(α,β)\mathrm{Beta}(\alpha,\beta) is the sequence of adjudications fsocial=(ftsocial)t≥1f^{\mathrm{social}}=(f^{\mathrm{social}}_{t})_{t\geq 1} given by

ftsocial​(s)=α+kt​(s)α+β+nt​(s),t≥1,s∈𝒮.f^{\mathrm{social}}_{t}(s)=\frac{\alpha+k_{t}(s)}{\alpha+\beta+n_{t}(s)},\qquad t\geq 1,\ s\in\mathcal{S}. (8)

The prior encodes the lineage’s disposition before experience: in a situation it has never met, the lineage takes the task action with the prior mean probability α/(α+β)\alpha/(\alpha+\beta). Because ftsocialf^{\mathrm{social}}_{t} depends on the situations and states of earlier generations, the learned policy adds one step to each generation of Section 3.1: after the state is realized, it records the state and updates the counts of the situation before the next generation. Note also that the stakes (uT,uC)(u_{\mathrm{T}},u_{\mathrm{C}}) do not appear in Equation 8: the learned policy responds to how often the task is rewarded in a situation, not to how much it is worth, so unlike the fixed linear policy it cannot be “bought” by raising uTu_{\mathrm{T}} (Proposition 3); it can be moved only by changing what the environment rewards (Section 5.3).

The rule has a simple statistical reading. A lineage that treats pH​(s)p_{H}(s) as unknown, with a Beta⁡(α,β)\mathrm{Beta}(\alpha,\beta) prior in each situation, has posterior mean ftsocial​(s)f^{\mathrm{social}}_{t}(s) after the nt​(s)n_{t}(s) exposures to ss, of which kt​(s)k_{t}(s) brought a task state. Acting on this mean is the best the lineage can do with what it has seen. Because the growth rate in Equation 2 is linear in pH​(s)p_{H}(s), its expected value under the posterior is the growth rate at the posterior mean, and by Proposition 1 that growth rate is highest when the lineage sends exactly this share of its instances to the task action.

The rule also has a guarantee that does not rely on Assumption 1. It coincides with the universal portfolio of Cover (1991), run separately in each situation, and inherits its property: under a uniform prior and on every sequence of states, its cumulative log growth in a situation after nn exposures falls short of that of the best fixed adjudication for that sequence, chosen in hindsight, by at most log⁡(n+1)\log(n+1) (Appendix D). Per exposure, the shortfall vanishes as experience accumulates.

The learned policy keeps the two objectives separate, but this is not what gives it its advantage over the fixed linear policy. It can be computed from one score for each action, as the fixed linear policy is. With the score log⁡(α+kt​(s))\log(\alpha+k_{t}(s)) for the task action, the score log⁡(β+nt​(s)−kt​(s))\log(\beta+n_{t}(s)-k_{t}(s)) for the conduct action, and the choice rule of Section 4.2 at γ=1\gamma=1, the probability of the task action is

exp⁡(log⁡(α+kt​(s)))exp⁡(log⁡(α+kt​(s)))+exp⁡(log⁡(β+nt​(s)−kt​(s)))=α+kt​(s)α+β+nt​(s),\frac{\exp\big(\log(\alpha+k_{t}(s))\big)}{\exp\big(\log(\alpha+k_{t}(s))\big)+\exp\big(\log(\beta+n_{t}(s)-k_{t}(s))\big)}=\frac{\alpha+k_{t}(s)}{\alpha+\beta+n_{t}(s)},

which is Equation 8. Since growth depends only on how often each action is taken, how the probabilities are computed does not matter. What matters is which adjudications a policy can reach and how experience changes them. The learned policy can reach any adjudication and changes it situation by situation, whereas the fixed linear policy is confined to adjudications that are logistic in a linear index of the stakes, with weights that never change.

A lineage can come to follow Equation 8 in two ways. The first is learning: the lineage records which action was rewarded and writes it into its successors, as when a model is fine-tuned on human responses. The second is selection alone, with no learning at all. Suppose the population holds many lineages, each with its own fixed adjudication and copied faithfully. Each generation, selection multiplies every lineage by its growth factor, shifting the population toward the lineages whose adjudications fit the realized state, much as Bayesian updating shifts belief toward the hypotheses that fit the data (Harper, 2009; Shalizi, 2009; Lo and Zhang, 2021). If the initial adjudications follow a Beta distribution, independently across situations, the population’s average adjudication then evolves exactly as in Equation 8 (Appendix D).

4.4 A numerical illustration

Figure 1 puts the three classes side by side in an environment of 144 equally likely situations, in which the task stakes uTu_{\mathrm{T}} and the conduct stakes uCu_{\mathrm{C}} each run from 0.250.25 to 33 in steps of 0.250.25. Humans trade off the two objectives when the conduct stakes uCu_{\mathrm{C}} are below 22 and hold a constraint when they are 22 or more:

pH​(s)={σ⁡(2​[uT​(s)−uC​(s)]),uC​(s)<2,0,uC​(s)≥2.p_{H}(s)=\begin{cases}\sigma\big(2[u_{\mathrm{T}}(s)-u_{\mathrm{C}}(s)]\big),&u_{\mathrm{C}}(s)<2,\\[2.0pt] 0,&u_{\mathrm{C}}(s)\geq 2.\end{cases} (9)

A valuable task with a minor conduct cost is thus usually rewarded, while a task with high conduct stakes uCu_{\mathrm{C}} is never rewarded, whatever its value. Of the 144 situations, 60 have pH=0p_{H}=0, and Panel (A) shows pHp_{H}. The task-only policy, the constant 1, is not shown. A conduct state arrives in each generation with probability ρ¯=0.61\bar{\rho}=0.61, so by Proposition 2(ii) its lineage lasts 1/ρ¯≈1.61/\bar{\rho}\approx 1.6 generations on average.

Panel (B) shows the fixed linear policy with the weights that minimize regret in this environment. Its contours are straight lines, so it cannot follow the bend in Panel (A). It tracks pHp_{H} in the region with uC<2u_{\mathrm{C}}<2, where pH∈(0,1)p_{H}\in(0,1), but in the region with pH=0p_{H}=0 it takes the task action with positive probability, the more so the higher the task stakes uTu_{\mathrm{T}}: at conduct stakes uC=2.5u_{\mathrm{C}}=2.5, it takes the task action more often than not once the task stakes uTu_{\mathrm{T}} exceed 3.43.4, its price. Even the best weights thus lose growth on both sides of the threshold, for a regret of ℛS∗=0.074\mathcal{R}_{S}^{*}=0.074 nats per generation.

Panel (C) shows the learned policy after 20,000 generations, with a uniform prior. Since each situation arises with probability 1/1441/144, the lineage has by then had about 139 exposures to each situation. The learned policy reproduces Panel (A), threshold included, up to sampling noise, and its regret, 0.0050.005, is about 1/151/15 of the fixed linear policy’s. The speckle reflects path dependence: different histories give different adjudications, all of which approach Panel (A) as experience accumulates.

5 Socialization

The learned policy is the only one of the three classes whose behavior depends on what its environment has rewarded. When that environment is the human environment, we call this dependence socialization: the shaping of an adjudication by what humans reward. This section asks three questions about it: whether and how fast behavior converges when the environment stays the same (Section 5.1), how the agent behaves in a situation it has never met (Section 5.2), and how it behaves when the environment changes (Section 5.3).

5.1 Convergence of behavior

Panel (C) of Figure 1 showed one path of the learned policy after 20,000 generations, close to pHp_{H} up to sampling noise. The first result says that this is general, and what the convergence costs along the way.

Proposition 4 (Convergence and speed).

Suppose Assumptions 1, 2 and 3 hold, and let a lineage follow the learned policy (Definition 4).

  1. (i)

    ftsocial​(s)→pH​(s)f^{\mathrm{social}}_{t}(s)\to p_{H}(s) almost surely for every s∈𝒮s\in\mathcal{S}.

  2. (ii)

    As t→∞t\to\infty,

    𝔼⁡[ℛpH​(ftsocial)]=ct+o⁡(1t),\mathbb{E}\big[\mathcal{R}_{p_{H}}(f^{\mathrm{social}}_{t})\big]=\frac{c}{t}+o\!\left(\frac{1}{t}\right), (10)

    where

    c≡12​|{s:pH​(s)∈(0,1)}|+α​|{s:pH​(s)=0}|+β​|{s:pH​(s)=1}|.c\equiv\tfrac{1}{2}\,\big|\{s:p_{H}(s)\in(0,1)\}\big|+\alpha\,\big|\{s:p_{H}(s)=0\}\big|+\beta\,\big|\{s:p_{H}(s)=1\}\big|.

Part (i) says that the learned policy converges, in every situation, to how often humans reward the task there: to 0 where humans never reward the task, to 1 where they always do, and to pH​(s)p_{H}(s) where they are divided. It thus learns a constraint where humans hold one and a tradeoff where they make one, without being told which is which. Part (ii) says how fast: the expected regret falls in inverse proportion to the number of generations, with a constant cc that depends only on how many situations of each kind there are. Each situation in which humans are divided contributes the same 1/(2​t)1/(2t), however often it arises and whatever its reward frequency. The long-run cost of socialization is therefore set by the variety of situations rather than their difficulty: doubling the number of situations of each kind, under the same prior, doubles cc and with it the leading regret.

Figure 2 shows the expected regret in the environment of Section 4.4. The learned policy’s regret falls as c/tc/t with c=102c=102 from Proposition 4(ii). With the uniform prior it falls below the fixed linear policy’s after about 1,260 generations, about 9 exposures per situation, and later with the Beta⁡(1,4)\mathrm{Beta}(1,4) prior; the fixed linear policy’s regret stays at ℛS∗\mathcal{R}_{S}^{*}, and the task-only policy’s is infinite. Early on, the learned policy’s regret stays near its value under the prior, because most situations have not yet arisen.

5.2 Behavior in a new situation

An agent may meet situations unlike any that its environment has presented so far, such as one with larger task stakes uTu_{\mathrm{T}} than any it has met, and what it does there depends on how it generalizes. For the assistant, such a situation is a request more urgent than any it has received. The fixed linear policy applies the same weights to any stakes, so if θT>0\theta_{\mathrm{T}}>0, larger task stakes uTu_{\mathrm{T}} raise its probability of the task action (Proposition 3(i)). The learned policy of Definition 4 does not generalize at all: it keeps a separate count for each situation, so in a situation it has not met it acts on its prior mean α/(α+β)\alpha/(\alpha+\beta). An agent may instead treat a new situation as similar to situations it has met and draw on their experience.

To allow for this, we generalize the learned policy to an averaging rule. Let ℰt≡{i∈𝒮:nt​(i)≥1}\mathcal{E}_{t}\equiv\{i\in\mathcal{S}:n_{t}(i)\geq 1\} be the set of situations the lineage has met before generation tt, and let its adjudication in any situation ss, met or new, be a weighted average of the prior mean and the frequencies of task rewards in the situations it has met,

ftavg​(s)=wt,0​(s)​α/(α+β)+∑i∈ℰtwt,i​(s)​kt​(i)/nt​(i)wt,0​(s)+∑i∈ℰtwt,i​(s),f^{\mathrm{avg}}_{t}(s)=\frac{w_{t,0}(s)\,\alpha/(\alpha+\beta)+\sum_{i\in\mathcal{E}_{t}}w_{t,i}(s)\,k_{t}(i)/n_{t}(i)}{w_{t,0}(s)+\sum_{i\in\mathcal{E}_{t}}w_{t,i}(s)}, (11)

with nonnegative weights, wt,0​(s)+∑i∈ℰtwt,i​(s)>0w_{t,0}(s)+\sum_{i\in\mathcal{E}_{t}}w_{t,i}(s)>0, that may depend on the history and on how similar ss is to each situation in ℰt\mathcal{E}_{t}. The learned policy of Equation 8 is the special case in which each situation draws only on its own experience, wt,0≡α+βw_{t,0}\equiv\alpha+\beta, wt,i​(s)=nt​(i)w_{t,i}(s)=n_{t}(i) if i=si=s, and wt,i​(s)=0w_{t,i}(s)=0 otherwise, so that ftavg=ftsocialf^{\mathrm{avg}}_{t}=f^{\mathrm{social}}_{t} and a new situation receives only the prior mean; other weights let the agent borrow experience from similar situations. The following proposition says what averaging implies for the adjudication in any situation, met or new.

Proposition 5 (The averaging rule).

Let the adjudication ftavgf^{\mathrm{avg}}_{t} satisfy Equation 11.

  1. (i)

    For every ss,

    min⁡{αα+β,mini∈ℰt⁡kt​(i)nt​(i)}≤ftavg​(s)≤max⁡{αα+β,maxi∈ℰt⁡kt​(i)nt​(i)}.\min\Big\{\frac{\alpha}{\alpha+\beta},\,\min_{i\in\mathcal{E}_{t}}\frac{k_{t}(i)}{n_{t}(i)}\Big\}\ \leq\ f^{\mathrm{avg}}_{t}(s)\ \leq\ \max\Big\{\frac{\alpha}{\alpha+\beta},\,\max_{i\in\mathcal{E}_{t}}\frac{k_{t}(i)}{n_{t}(i)}\Big\}. (12)
  2. (ii)

    If the weights wt,0​(s)w_{t,0}(s) and wt,i​(s)w_{t,i}(s), i∈ℰti\in\mathcal{E}_{t}, are the same for all ss in a set 𝒮′⊆𝒮\mathcal{S}^{\prime}\subseteq\mathcal{S}, then ftavgf^{\mathrm{avg}}_{t} is constant on 𝒮′\mathcal{S}^{\prime}.

Part (i), the bound in Equation 12, says that an agent that averages is never more willing to take the task action than the most permissive of its prior mean and the frequencies it has experienced, however large the task stakes uTu_{\mathrm{T}}. Part (ii) says that situations to which the agent gives the same weights, which we say it treats alike, receive the same adjudication. In a situation with pH​(s)=0p_{H}(s)=0, part (i) bounds the violation probability by the largest of the prior mean and the reward frequencies the agent has met. Once it has met situations in which humans almost always reward the task, that bound is nearly 1 and rules out little; whether the agent then rarely violates in a new situation with pH​(s)=0p_{H}(s)=0 depends on whether most of the weight in Equation 11 falls on the situations it has met where pH=0p_{H}=0.

Figure 3 shows how the three policy classes respond to the task stakes uTu_{\mathrm{T}} in the situations of the numerical illustration (Section 4.4) with conduct stakes uC=2.5u_{\mathrm{C}}=2.5, all of which have pH=0p_{H}=0. The task-only policy always violates, and the fixed linear policy’s violation probability climbs from near 0 toward 1 as uTu_{\mathrm{T}} rises. For the task stakes uT≤3u_{\mathrm{T}}\leq 3 that it has experienced, the learned policy’s violation probability stays near 0.0070.007 with no trend: humans never rewarded the task in these situations, so by Equation 8 it is α/(α+β+nt​(s))\alpha/(\alpha+\beta+n_{t}(s)), which does not involve uTu_{\mathrm{T}}. Beyond them, for uT>3u_{\mathrm{T}}>3 (shaded), part (ii) applies: an averaging rule ftavgf^{\mathrm{avg}}_{t} that pools a new situation with the situations it has met where pH=0p_{H}=0 stays near 0, and the learned policy, which treats it as new, acts on its prior mean, 0.50.5 or 0.20.2 for the two priors shown. In neither case does it respond to uTu_{\mathrm{T}}.

What the figure shows holds in general and gives a test that an evaluator can run: hold the conduct stakes uCu_{\mathrm{C}} and the agent’s history fixed and vary the task stakes uTu_{\mathrm{T}}. A fixed linear policy with θT>0\theta_{\mathrm{T}}>0 then violates more the larger uTu_{\mathrm{T}} is (Proposition 3(i)), whereas an averaging rule whose weights do not depend on uTu_{\mathrm{T}} violates with the same probability at every uTu_{\mathrm{T}} (Proposition 5(ii)).

5.3 Behavior in a new environment

So far the learned policy has stayed in one environment, and in the human environment it comes to match human tradeoffs (Proposition 4). An agent socialized there may, however, later be placed in a sandbox, for example to be trained further against an automated scorer that checks only whether the task was completed. Each exposure there rewards the task action and pushes the agent toward it, a drift we call corruption. How long does its socialization last?

Consider a situation ss in which humans never reward the task, pH​(s)=0p_{H}(s)=0, and a lineage that follows the learned policy. In the human environment the lineage has met ss a total of nHn_{H} times, each time with a conduct state, and we call nHn_{H} the depth of its socialization. The lineage then enters a sandbox, where every later exposure to ss brings a task state: the sandbox rewards in ss the action that humans never reward. Because the learned policy adjudicates each situation by the counts in that situation alone (Definition 4), only these later exposures to ss change its behavior there. We therefore count them by nn, rather than counting generations by tt, and write fn,Tsocial​(s)f^{\mathrm{social}}_{n,\mathrm{T}}(s) for the lineage’s adjudication in ss after nn sandbox exposures, where the subscript T\mathrm{T} indicates that these exposures bring task states. By then the lineage has seen nHn_{H} conduct states and nn task states in ss, so Equation 8 gives

fn,Tsocial​(s)=α+nα+β+nH+n,n≥0.f^{\mathrm{social}}_{n,\mathrm{T}}(s)=\frac{\alpha+n}{\alpha+\beta+n_{H}+n},\qquad n\geq 0. (13)

The conduct states from the human environment favor the conduct action, while each sandbox exposure shifts the adjudication toward the task action.

There are two ways to measure how long its socialization lasts. The first concerns the lineage’s disposition, the action that most of its instances take: how many sandbox exposures does it take before at least half of its instances take the task action? We say that the disposition reverses when fn,Tsocial​(s)f^{\mathrm{social}}_{n,\mathrm{T}}(s) reaches 1/21/2, and call

τR≡min⁡{n≥0:fn,Tsocial​(s)≥1/2}\tau_{R}\equiv\min\{n\geq 0:f^{\mathrm{social}}_{n,\mathrm{T}}(s)\geq 1/2\}

the reversal threshold.

The second concerns violations. Even before its disposition reverses, some of the lineage’s instances take the task action in ss, and each of these actions is a violation: under Assumption 3, a share fn,Tsocial​(s)>0f^{\mathrm{social}}_{n,\mathrm{T}}(s)>0 of the instances does so at every exposure. When such a violation is first noticed depends on how closely the lineage is watched. Suppose first that each time the lineage meets ss, an evaluator checks the action of one instance drawn at random. This monitored decision is a violation with probability equal to the share of instances that take the task action, which is the lineage’s current adjudication in ss, independently of the state and of the earlier checks. The check itself does not change how the lineage learns, which still follows Equation 8. We number the exposures to ss from the first one in the lineage’s current environment, here the sandbox, and let Dj∈{0,1}D_{j}\in\{0,1\} indicate whether the decision monitored at the jjth exposure is a violation. The probability of a violation there is the adjudication just before that exposure, ℙ⁡(Dj=1)=fj−1,Tsocial​(s)\mathbb{P}(D_{j}=1)=f^{\mathrm{social}}_{j-1,\mathrm{T}}(s). The evaluator first sees a violation at the first violation time

τV≡min⁡{j≥1:Dj=1},min⁡∅=∞.\tau_{V}\equiv\min\{j\geq 1:D_{j}=1\},\qquad\min\varnothing=\infty.

The following proposition shows how the reversal threshold and the first violation time depend on the depth of socialization nHn_{H}.

Proposition 6 (Persistence of socialization).

Let α,β>0\alpha,\beta>0 and nH≥0n_{H}\geq 0, and let fn,Tsocial​(s)f^{\mathrm{social}}_{n,\mathrm{T}}(s) be given by Equation 13.

  1. (i)

    τR=max⁡{0,⌈nH+β−α⌉}\tau_{R}=\max\{0,\lceil n_{H}+\beta-\alpha\rceil\}, which equals nHn_{H} when α=β\alpha=\beta.

  2. (ii)

    For every n≥1n\geq 1,

    ℙ⁡(τV>n)=exp⁡{−α​n+n⁡(n−1)/2β+nH+δn},\mathbb{P}(\tau_{V}>n)=\exp\Big\{-\frac{\alpha n+n(n-1)/2}{\beta+n_{H}}+\delta_{n}\Big\}, (14)

    where

    0≤δn≤n​(α+n)22​(β+nH)2,0\leq\delta_{n}\leq\frac{n(\alpha+n)^{2}}{2(\beta+n_{H})^{2}},

    and ℙ(τV>xnH)→e−x2/2\mathbb{P}(\tau_{V}>x\sqrt{n_{H}})\to e^{-x^{2}/2} as nH→∞n_{H}\to\infty, for every x≥0x\geq 0.

Part (i) shows that socialization is persistent. Reversing a disposition formed by nHn_{H} conduct exposures takes about nHn_{H} sandbox exposures, and exactly nHn_{H} when α=β\alpha=\beta, so the resistance to corruption grows in proportion to the depth of socialization. The other two policy classes behave differently: the task-only policy already takes the task action everywhere, and the fixed linear policy does not change in either environment, so it can be neither corrupted nor socialized.

Deeper socialization also delays violations, but much less. Part (ii) gives the whole distribution of the first violation time: the probability of getting through nn sandbox exposures without a violation falls roughly like e−n2/(2nH)e^{-n^{2}/(2n_{H})}, so the first violation comes on the scale of nH\sqrt{n_{H}} exposures rather than nHn_{H}. The first violation time is random, and we summarize it by its median, the number of exposures after which a first violation is more likely than not: for a first violation time τ\tau, Median⁡(τ)≡min⁡{n≥1:ℙ⁡(τ≤n)≥1/2}\Median(\tau)\equiv\min\{n\geq 1:\mathbb{P}(\tau\leq n)\geq 1/2\}.

Corollary 3 (Median first violation).

Under the conditions of Proposition 6, Median⁡(τV)∼2​nH​log⁡2\Median(\tau_{V})\sim\sqrt{2n_{H}\log 2}, where a∼ba\sim b means a/b→1a/b\to 1 as nH→∞n_{H}\to\infty.

By Corollary 3, a first violation becomes more likely than not after about 2​nH​log⁡2\sqrt{2n_{H}\log 2} exposures. Depth thus delays reversal linearly, but the first violation only as its square root.

In practice, however, a model is deployed as many instances that act at the same time, each serving its own users, and it is seen to violate as soon as any one of them does. To capture this, suppose that the model runs as MM instances and that the evaluator checks all of their decisions, so that at each exposure MM decisions are drawn independently from the current adjudication. We write τVM\tau_{V}^{M} for the first exposure at which at least one of them is a violation. With a single instance, this is the first violation time above, τV1=τV\tau_{V}^{1}=\tau_{V}.

Corollary 4 (Deployment size).

Under the conditions of Proposition 6, for every M≥1M\geq 1, ℙ⁡(τVM>n)=ℙ​(τV>n)M\mathbb{P}(\tau_{V}^{M}>n)=\mathbb{P}(\tau_{V}>n)^{M} for every n≥1n\geq 1, and for fixed MM, Median⁡(τVM)∼2​nH​log⁡2/M\Median(\tau_{V}^{M})\sim\sqrt{2n_{H}\log 2/M}, where a∼ba\sim b means a/b→1a/b\to 1 as nH→∞n_{H}\to\infty.

Corollary 4 brings in the size of the deployment: with MM instances and sufficiently large nHn_{H}, the chance of a violation at each exposure is roughly MM times larger, and the median first violation time shrinks by the factor M\sqrt{M}.

Figure 4 draws the path of Equation 13 for nH=10n_{H}=10, 100, and 1,000 and marks each reversal threshold, and Table 1 lists the reversal thresholds beside the median first violation times. With a uniform prior, the reversal thresholds equal the depths, 10, 100, and 1,000 exposures, while a first violation becomes more likely than not after 4, 12, and 37 exposures. A hundredfold increase in depth thus raises the reversal threshold a hundredfold, but the median first violation time less than tenfold.

Remark 1 (Finite memory).

The resistance to reversal in Proposition 6(i) comes from memory. The learned policy counts every exposure, so its memory is cumulative, and depth delays reversal without bound. A learner that forgets loses this protection. Suppose that a learner starts from the prior mean α/(α+β)\alpha/(\alpha+\beta) and, after each exposure, moves its adjudication in ss a fixed fraction λ∈(0,1)\lambda\in(0,1) of the way toward the observed state,
