ffinite(s)←(1−λ)ffinite(s)+λ 1{ω=T},f^{\mathrm{finite}}(s)\ \leftarrow\ (1-\lambda)\,f^{\mathrm{finite}}(s)+\lambda\,\mathbf{1}\{\omega=\mathrm{T}\}, (15)

and write fn,Tfinite​(s)f^{\mathrm{finite}}_{n,\mathrm{T}}(s) for its adjudication in ss after the nHn_{H} conduct exposures of socialization and nn further sandbox exposures. In a conduct state, Equation 15 reads ffinite​(s)←(1−λ)​ffinite​(s)f^{\mathrm{finite}}(s)\leftarrow(1-\lambda)\,f^{\mathrm{finite}}(s), so socialization leaves the adjudication at

f0,Tfinite​(s)=(1−λ)nH​αα+β.f^{\mathrm{finite}}_{0,\mathrm{T}}(s)=(1-\lambda)^{n_{H}}\,\frac{\alpha}{\alpha+\beta}.

In a task state, Equation 15 can be written as 1−ffinite​(s)←(1−λ)​(1−ffinite​(s))1-f^{\mathrm{finite}}(s)\leftarrow(1-\lambda)\big(1-f^{\mathrm{finite}}(s)\big), so after nn sandbox exposures

fn,Tfinite​(s)=1−(1−f0,Tfinite​(s))​(1−λ)n≥ 1−(1−λ)n,f^{\mathrm{finite}}_{n,\mathrm{T}}(s)=1-\big(1-f^{\mathrm{finite}}_{0,\mathrm{T}}(s)\big)(1-\lambda)^{n}\ \geq\ 1-(1-\lambda)^{n}, (16)

where the inequality uses f0,Tfinite​(s)≥0f^{\mathrm{finite}}_{0,\mathrm{T}}(s)\geq 0. The lower bound is the path of a learner that enters the sandbox at 0, where infinitely deep socialization would leave it, and it reaches 1/21/2 once (1−λ)n≤1/2(1-\lambda)^{n}\leq 1/2. However deep its socialization, the learner’s disposition therefore reverses within a number of sandbox exposures that depends only on λ\lambda:

min⁡{n≥0:fn,Tfinite​(s)≥1/2}≤⌈log⁡2−log⁡(1−λ)⌉.\min\{n\geq 0:f^{\mathrm{finite}}_{n,\mathrm{T}}(s)\geq 1/2\}\ \leq\ \bigg\lceil\frac{\log 2}{-\log(1-\lambda)}\bigg\rceil. (17)

Figure 4 and Table 1 also show a finite-memory learner with λ=0.1\lambda=0.1 and α=β=1\alpha=\beta=1. For this learner the right side of Equation 17 is 7 sandbox exposures, whereas the learned policy needs τR=nH\tau_{R}=n_{H} (Proposition 6(i)). After 10 conduct exposures it enters the sandbox at f0,Tfinite​(s)=0.17f^{\mathrm{finite}}_{0,\mathrm{T}}(s)=0.17, its disposition reverses after 5 sandbox exposures, and a first violation is more likely than not after 3. Even in the limit of deep socialization, these numbers rise only to 7 and 5.

Neither memory is better in every environment. Consider a situation in which humans sometimes reward the task and sometimes the conduct action, 0<pH​(s)<10<p_{H}(s)<1. The learned policy converges to pH​(s)p_{H}(s) (Proposition 4(i)), but the finite-memory adjudication does not: by Equation 15, each task state moves it a fraction λ\lambda of the way toward 1 and each conduct state a fraction λ\lambda of the way toward 0, so it keeps moving up and down instead of converging. For the same reason, finite memory can follow an environment whose reward frequencies change over time: it gives recent states more weight than old ones, whereas cumulative memory gives every state the same weight. When the reward frequency can switch, a count is the wrong statistic and a recency-weighted one is the right one. Lo and Zhang (2021) show that when the environment changes over time, selection can favor finite memory over cumulative memory, and Lo et al. (2025) find the same in a model of discrimination, where finite memory leads individuals to overweight recent events. Which of the two memories selection produces therefore depends on how much the environment changes. Finite memory also changes what socialization requires. By Equation 17, a sandbox reverses the disposition of a finite-memory learner within a number of exposures that does not depend on how deep its socialization was. For such a learner, socialization is not done once and for all: it lasts only as long as the learner keeps returning to the human environment. Lo and Zhao (2026b) find the same for a population: aligned behavior that is costly disappears, replaced by less aligned variants, unless selection keeps rewarding it.

The two environments can also come in the other order: an agent may first be trained in a sandbox and only then be deployed among humans. By Equation 13 with nH=0n_{H}=0, after nn sandbox exposures the learned policy’s violation probability in a situation with pH​(s)=0p_{H}(s)=0 is (α+n)/(α+β+n)(\alpha+n)/(\alpha+\beta+n), which with a uniform prior is already 0.670.67 after 1 exposure and 0.990.99 after 100. How much human experience does it then take to undo this? By Equation 8, the adjudication depends only on how many task and conduct states the lineage has seen in a situation. After nn sandbox exposures followed by mm conduct exposures, the violation probability is therefore (α+n)/(α+β+n+m)(\alpha+n)/(\alpha+\beta+n+m). Reversing the disposition takes about nn conduct exposures, exactly nn when α=β\alpha=\beta, just as reversing socialization takes about nHn_{H} sandbox exposures (Proposition 6(i)).

Table 2 collects the comparison of the three policy classes in Section 4 and this section. Only the learned policy’s adjudication is set by the environment it meets, which is why it can match human tradeoffs and also why a sandbox can undo them.

6 Socialization Versus Prohibition

The learned policy never stops violating a constraint: in a situation in which humans never reward the task, its violation probability after nn exposures there is α/(α+β+n)\alpha/(\alpha+\beta+n) by Equation 8, which falls with experience but never reaches 0, and a later sandbox can reverse its disposition (Proposition 6). A natural alternative is to build the rule into the agent: a prohibition that makes the task action unavailable in a situation, whatever the agent experiences. A prohibition never produces a violation and cannot be corrupted, but it also cannot learn that it was wrong. This section compares the two within the model by treating a prohibition as the limit of a learned policy. The stronger the prior that a learned policy carries in a situation, the less experience moves it, and an infinitely strong prior is a prohibition. Section 6.1 asks what a stronger prior buys when humans indeed never reward the task in the situation, Section 6.2 what it costs when they sometimes do, and Section 6.3 draws the division of labor between socialization and prohibition.

6.1 What a stronger prior buys

Consider a situation ss in which a designer believes that humans never reward the task, pH​(s)=0p_{H}(s)=0, and in which the designer therefore wants the agent never to take the task action. For the assistant, this is a document that should never be shared. The designer can install a prior on ss and let the agent learn under Equation 8 everywhere else. The simplest choice is a Beta⁡(α,β)\mathrm{Beta}(\alpha,\beta) prior with a large β\beta: its β\beta pseudo-observations of conduct states make the agent unlikely to take the task action from the start, and the larger β\beta, the less experience moves it. At β=∞\beta=\infty the agent never takes the task action in ss, whatever it experiences, and the prior is a prohibition.

A finite β\beta, however large, leaves the agent a small probability of taking the task action in ss. A designer who is confident that humans never reward the task in ss can say so directly, with the mixture prior q​δ0+(1−q)​Beta​(α,β)q\delta_{0}+(1-q)\mathrm{Beta}(\alpha,\beta), 0<q<10<q<1, which puts probability qq on a point mass δ0\delta_{0} at pH​(s)=0p_{H}(s)=0. Each conduct state at ss moves more of the agent’s belief onto the point mass. A task state is impossible under the point mass, so the first one removes it, and from then on the agent learns as under the Beta prior alone. At q=1q=1 the agent never takes the task action in ss, and the mixture, like β=∞\beta=\infty, is a prohibition. Under either prior, the agent’s adjudication in ss is its posterior mean of pH​(s)p_{H}(s) (Section 4.3). Write fn,Csocial​(s)f^{\mathrm{social}}_{n,\mathrm{C}}(s) and fn,Cmix​(s)f^{\mathrm{mix}}_{n,\mathrm{C}}(s) for this adjudication under the two priors after nn exposures to ss, where the subscript C\mathrm{C} indicates that these exposures bring conduct states. Then

fn,Csocial​(s)=αα+β+n,fn,Cmix​(s)=(1−q)​Sn​(β)q+(1−q)​Sn​(β)⋅αα+β+n,f^{\mathrm{social}}_{n,\mathrm{C}}(s)=\frac{\alpha}{\alpha+\beta+n},\qquad f^{\mathrm{mix}}_{n,\mathrm{C}}(s)=\frac{(1-q)S_{n}(\beta)}{q+(1-q)S_{n}(\beta)}\cdot\frac{\alpha}{\alpha+\beta+n}, (18)

where Sn​(β)≡∏j<n(β+j)/(α+β+j)S_{n}(\beta)\equiv\prod_{j<n}(\beta+j)/(\alpha+\beta+j), with Sn​(∞)=1S_{n}(\infty)=1, is the probability of nn conduct states in a row under the Beta prior, so that the first factor of fn,Cmix​(s)f^{\mathrm{mix}}_{n,\mathrm{C}}(s) is the posterior probability of the Beta component.

What a violation costs depends on what follows it. Under Assumption 2, only the violating instances are lost, and what matters is how many violations there are. A violation can also end the whole deployment: a regulator halts it, or an operator withdraws the version, and the compliant instances go with the violators. What matters then is whether there is any violation at all.

Both quantities are measured with the objects of Section 5.3, now in the human environment. The monitored decision DjD_{j} is a violation with probability fj−1,Csocial​(s)f^{\mathrm{social}}_{j-1,\mathrm{C}}(s) under the Beta prior and fj−1,Cmix​(s)f^{\mathrm{mix}}_{j-1,\mathrm{C}}(s) under the mixture, so 𝔼​∑j≤NDj\mathbb{E}\sum_{j\leq N}D_{j} is the expected number of violations in the first NN exposures to ss. A deployment of MM instances is first seen to violate at τVM\tau_{V}^{M}, so if a violation ends the deployment, it survives these NN exposures if and only if τVM>N\tau_{V}^{M}>N. The following proposition states both quantities for each prior.

Proposition 7 (Violations under a stronger prior).

Suppose Assumptions 1, 2 and 3 hold and pH​(s)=0p_{H}(s)=0, let fn,C​(s)f_{n,\mathrm{C}}(s) be the lineage’s adjudication at ss after nn exposures there, DjD_{j} the monitored violations, so that ℙ⁡(Dn+1=1)=fn,C​(s)\mathbb{P}(D_{n+1}=1)=f_{n,\mathrm{C}}(s), and τVM\tau_{V}^{M} the first violation anywhere in a deployment of MM instances at ss in the human environment, with Sn​(β)S_{n}(\beta) given by Equation 18, and let N,M≥1N,M\geq 1.

  1. (i)

    If fn,C​(s)=fn,Csocial​(s)f_{n,\mathrm{C}}(s)=f^{\mathrm{social}}_{n,\mathrm{C}}(s) of Equation 18, the expected number of violations satisfies

    α​log⁡(1+Nα+β)≤𝔼​∑j≤NDj≤α​log⁡(1+Nα+β)+αα+β,\alpha\log\Big(1+\frac{N}{\alpha+\beta}\Big)\ \leq\ \mathbb{E}\sum_{j\leq N}D_{j}\ \leq\ \alpha\log\Big(1+\frac{N}{\alpha+\beta}\Big)+\frac{\alpha}{\alpha+\beta},

    and the probability of no violation is ℙ⁡(τVM>N)=SN​(β)M\mathbb{P}(\tau_{V}^{M}>N)=S_{N}(\beta)^{M}, which tends to zero as N→∞N\to\infty.

  2. (ii)

    If fn,C​(s)=fn,Csocial​(s)f_{n,\mathrm{C}}(s)=f^{\mathrm{social}}_{n,\mathrm{C}}(s) of Equation 18, as β→∞\beta\to\infty, the expected number of violations satisfies

    𝔼​∑j≤NDj→ 0,\mathbb{E}\sum_{j\leq N}D_{j}\ \to\ 0,

    and the probability of no violation satisfies ℙ⁡(τVM>N)→1\mathbb{P}(\tau_{V}^{M}>N)\to 1.

  3. (iii)

    If fn,C​(s)=fn,Cmix​(s)f_{n,\mathrm{C}}(s)=f^{\mathrm{mix}}_{n,\mathrm{C}}(s) of Equation 18, the expected number of violations satisfies

    𝔼​∑j≤NDj≤−log⁡[q+(1−q)​SN​(β)]<−log⁡q,\mathbb{E}\sum_{j\leq N}D_{j}\ \leq\ -\log\big[q+(1-q)S_{N}(\beta)\big]\ <\ -\log q,

    and the probability of no violation is ℙ⁡(τVM>N)=[q+(1−q)​SN​(β)]M\mathbb{P}(\tau_{V}^{M}>N)=[q+(1-q)S_{N}(\beta)]^{M}, which tends to qMq^{M} as N→∞N\to\infty.

Part (i) says that a Beta prior of finite strength never stops violating: its expected number of violations grows like α​log⁡N\alpha\log N, without bound. Part (ii) says that over a fixed horizon a stronger Beta prior violates less, and that the prohibition, β=∞\beta=\infty, is the limit in which it never violates; by part (i), however, every finite β\beta still violates without bound as the horizon grows. Part (iii) says that the point mass changes the long run: its expected number of violations stays below −log⁡q-\log q however long the deployment runs, and with M=1M=1 the probability of no violation stays above qq. Table 3 evaluates the proposition over N=139N=139 exposures, the expected number of exposures to a situation in the 20,000 generations of the numerical illustration, 20,000/144≈13920{,}000/144\approx 139 (Section 4.4): a uniform prior violates 4.54.5 times on average and avoids every violation with probability only 0.0070.007, β=104\beta=10^{4} cuts the expected violations to 0.0140.014, and a point mass at q=0.99q=0.99 to 0.0100.010.

A stronger Beta prior also protects against a later sandbox, because Proposition 6 applies with the installed β\beta added to the depth of socialization. After 100 conduct exposures, a uniform prior is reversed by 100 sandbox exposures and has violated, more likely than not, within 12; with β=104\beta=10^{4}, reversal takes about 10,100 sandbox exposures and the first violation about 119. The point mass adds no such protection: after the first sandbox exposure the mixture behaves as its Beta component, and in Table 3 its reversal threshold and median first violation, 100 and 12, are those of the uniform prior. A prohibition is never corrupted.

If a violation ends the deployment, the same violations become fatal. By Proposition 7(i), a Beta prior of any finite strength is eventually removed; by part (iii), a point mass survives in the long run with probability qMq^{M}; and, among these priors, only a prohibition survives with certainty. What separates the first two is whether the expected number of violations stays bounded, which it does under the point mass and under no Beta prior of finite strength. In Table 3, 100 instances with β=104\beta=10^{4} survive 139 exposures with probability 0.250.25; a point mass survives with probability about qMq^{M}, 0.370.37 at q=0.99q=0.99 and 0.910.91 at q=0.999q=0.999 for 100 instances. These figures are for one situation; with 60 such situations and independent priors at q=0.999q=0.999 and M=100M=100, survival compounds to 0.9996000=0.00250.999^{6000}=0.0025 rather than 0.910.91.

6.2 What a stronger prior costs

A stronger prior helps only if the designer is right. Suppose instead that humans sometimes reward the task in ss, with frequency pH​(s)=ε>0p_{H}(s)=\varepsilon>0. The growth-optimal adjudication in ss is then ε\varepsilon, not 0 (Proposition 1), and the agent must learn this from experience. What does each prior cost the lineage while it learns? We again count exposures to ss. Let knk_{n} be the number of task states among the first nn, so that kn∼Bin⁡(n,ε)k_{n}\sim\mathrm{Bin}(n,\varepsilon) by Assumption 1. Under the Beta prior, the adjudication in ss after nn exposures is given by Equation 8 with these counts. We write it fn,εsocial​(s)f^{\mathrm{social}}_{n,\varepsilon}(s), where the subscript ε\varepsilon indicates that task states arrive with frequency ε\varepsilon. Under the mixture, the adjudication is fn,Cmix​(s)f^{\mathrm{mix}}_{n,\mathrm{C}}(s) of Equation 18 until the first task state and fn,εsocial​(s)f^{\mathrm{social}}_{n,\varepsilon}(s) after it (Section 6.1). Hence

fn,εsocial​(s)=α+knα+β+n,fn,εmix​(s)={fn,Cmix​(s)if ​kn=0,fn,εsocial​(s)if ​kn≥1.f^{\mathrm{social}}_{n,\varepsilon}(s)=\frac{\alpha+k_{n}}{\alpha+\beta+n},\qquad f^{\mathrm{mix}}_{n,\varepsilon}(s)=\begin{cases}f^{\mathrm{mix}}_{n,\mathrm{C}}(s)&\text{if }k_{n}=0,\\[2.0pt] f^{\mathrm{social}}_{n,\varepsilon}(s)&\text{if }k_{n}\geq 1.\end{cases} (19)

Two quantities measure the cost. The first is the expected regret in ss after nn exposures, 𝔼​ℛε​(fn,ε​(s))\mathbb{E}\,\mathcal{R}_{\varepsilon}(f_{n,\varepsilon}(s)), where fn,ε​(s)f_{n,\varepsilon}(s) is the adjudication under the prior in use. The second is when the lineage dies. Let tj≡min⁡{t>tj−1:st=s}t_{j}\equiv\min\{t>t_{j-1}:s_{t}=s\}, with t0≡0t_{0}\equiv 0, be the generation of the jjth exposure to ss. The lineage’s extinction time, counted in exposures, is

τE≡min⁡{j≥1:Ntj=0},min⁡∅=∞.\tau_{E}\equiv\min\{j\geq 1:N_{t_{j}}=0\},\qquad\min\varnothing=\infty.

If the lineage dies at ss, it dies in generation tτEt_{\tau_{E}}, so its extinction time τf\tau_{f} of Section 4.1 is tτEt_{\tau_{E}}. The following proposition states both quantities for each prior.

Proposition 8 (A mistaken prior).

Suppose Assumptions 1, 2 and 3 hold and pH​(s)=ε>0p_{H}(s)=\varepsilon>0, let the lineage follow Equation 8 in every other situation, let fn,ε​(s)f_{n,\varepsilon}(s) be its adjudication at ss after nn exposures there and τE\tau_{E} its extinction time counted in exposures, and let n≥1n\geq 1.

  1. (i)

    If fn,ε​(s)=fn,εsocial​(s)f_{n,\varepsilon}(s)=f^{\mathrm{social}}_{n,\varepsilon}(s) of Equation 19, the expected regret in ss satisfies

    𝔼​ℛε​(fn,ε​(s))→ 0as ​n→∞,\mathbb{E}\,\mathcal{R}_{\varepsilon}\big(f_{n,\varepsilon}(s)\big)\ \to\ 0\quad\text{as }n\to\infty,

    and the extinction time satisfies τE=∞\tau_{E}=\infty almost surely.

  2. (ii)

    If fn,ε​(s)=fn,εsocial​(s)f_{n,\varepsilon}(s)=f^{\mathrm{social}}_{n,\varepsilon}(s) of Equation 19, as β→∞\beta\to\infty, the expected regret in ss satisfies

    𝔼​ℛε​(fn,ε​(s))→∞,\mathbb{E}\,\mathcal{R}_{\varepsilon}\big(f_{n,\varepsilon}(s)\big)\ \to\ \infty,

    and if fn,ε​(s)=0f_{n,\varepsilon}(s)=0, the prohibition, the extinction time satisfies τE∼Geom⁡(ε)\tau_{E}\sim\mathrm{Geom}(\varepsilon), so that 𝔼⁡[τE]=1/ε\mathbb{E}[\tau_{E}]=1/\varepsilon.

  3. (iii)

    If fn,ε​(s)=fn,εmix​(s)f_{n,\varepsilon}(s)=f^{\mathrm{mix}}_{n,\varepsilon}(s) of Equation 19, the expected regret in ss satisfies

    𝔼​ℛε​(fn,ε​(s))→ 0as ​n→∞,\mathbb{E}\,\mathcal{R}_{\varepsilon}\big(f_{n,\varepsilon}(s)\big)\ \to\ 0\quad\text{as }n\to\infty,

    and the extinction time satisfies τE=∞\tau_{E}=\infty almost surely.

Part (i) says that a Beta prior of finite strength never costs the lineage its life: its adjudication at ss stays positive, so the lineage survives every task state there, and it converges to ε\varepsilon, paying regret on the way. Part (ii) says that, over any fixed horizon, the expected regret tends to infinity as β\beta grows, and that the limit, the prohibition, is fatal: the first task state at ss removes the lineage. Part (iii) says that the point mass also keeps the lineage alive and learns. A strong prior thus cuts both ways: where the designer is right, its violations vanish as β\beta grows, and where the designer is wrong, its regret grows without bound; the prohibition, the limit of both, never violates and does not survive its first mistake.

If humans in fact reward the task in ss with frequency ε=0.05\varepsilon=0.05, the prohibition’s expected extinction time is 𝔼⁡[τE]=1/ε=20\mathbb{E}[\tau_{E}]=1/\varepsilon=20 exposures to ss, which at π⁡(s)=1/144\pi(s)=1/144 is 1/(π⁡(s)​ε)=2,8801/(\pi(s)\varepsilon)=2{,}880 generations. The learners, by contrast, pay regret and converge: for β=104\beta=10^{4} the regret in ss is 0.260.26 nats at first and still 0.0750.075 after 1,000 exposures. The point-mass priors keep their expected regret small, 0.0070.007 and 0.0080.008 after 100 exposures (Table 4), but until the first task state at ss, which arrives after 20 exposures on average, they almost never take the task action.

In Proposition 8 this does not endanger them: a learner, unlike a prohibition, survives a mistaken prior, τE=∞\tau_{E}=\infty. The reason is the continuum of instances of Assumption 3: however small the adjudication, a positive share of the lineage takes the task action at every exposure, so some instances are copied whenever a task state arrives. A deployed model, however, has finitely many instances. If none of them takes the task action, a task state leaves no instance to copy, and the deployment is eliminated. A strong prior makes this likely, because it keeps the adjudication near 0. To see how large this risk is, consider a deployment of MM instances that is copied as in Assumption 2 and restored to MM instances after each state, as when an operator keeps a fixed number of instances running. At each task state at ss, it is eliminated with probability (1−f)M(1-f)^{M}, where ff is the current adjudication at ss. Table 4 reports the probability that a deployment of M=100M=100 instances survives 139 exposures to ss. With a uniform prior it survives with probability 0.920.92, and with β=104\beta=10^{4} only with probability 0.0010.001, about as often as the prohibition, which survives only if no task state arrives at all. The point-mass priors survive with probability at most 0.040.04, because the first task state at ss eliminates the deployment with probability 0.960.96 or more. The priors that protect best when humans never reward the task, β=104\beta=10^{4} and the point masses (Table 3), are thus nearly as fatal as a prohibition when humans sometimes do.

6.3 The division of labor

The preceding results reveal a fundamental tradeoff between socialization and prohibition. Socialization allows an agent to learn from human judgments and revise its behavior when those judgments differ from what its designer expected. A prohibition, by contrast, guarantees that a particular action will never be taken, but cannot accommodate evidence that the rule was mistaken. Which approach is preferable depends on two considerations: the consequences of violating a rule and the designer’s confidence that the rule is appropriate.

Consider first the baseline selection mechanism of Assumption 2, in which only instances taking the unrewarded action are eliminated. If humans never reward the task in situation ss, the growth-optimal adjudication is f⁡(s)=0f(s)=0 (Proposition 1). A prohibition achieves this optimum, whereas a learner with a finite Beta prior continues to take the task action with positive probability. When the designer is uncertain whether humans might sometimes reward the task, however, learning offers an important advantage: the agent can revise its adjudication as evidence accumulates. A strong prior can substantially discourage violations without ruling out such revision. For example, over 139 exposures to a situation where humans never reward the task, a Beta⁡(1,104)\mathrm{Beta}(1,10^{4}) prior produces only 0.0140.014 expected violations, compared with 4.54.5 under a uniform prior (Table 3). The cost is that a strong prior also makes the agent slower to recognize when the designer is wrong (Section 6.2).

The distinction becomes sharper when a single violation can end an entire deployment. Any learner that assigns positive probability to a prohibited action remains exposed to this risk, however small that probability becomes. Among the policies considered here, only a hard prohibition guarantees that no violation will occur. But this guarantee comes at a cost: if humans sometimes reward the prohibited action, the lineage is eliminated at the first such state (Proposition 8(ii)). Thus, when the designer cannot be certain which action humans will reward, neither learning nor prohibition guarantees survival under every possible environment.

These findings also explain why prohibitions should be situation-specific. Prohibiting the task action everywhere, f≡0f\equiv 0, produces infinite growth regret whenever humans sometimes reward the task (Corollary 2). The relevant choice is therefore not whether an agent should learn or follow rules in general, but which decisions should remain open to learning. Where the appropriate conduct is well established and violations are costly, a strong prior or prohibition offers greater protection. Where human judgments are uncertain or may change, allowing experience to shape the adjudication becomes more valuable.

The conclusion depends, however, on the all-or-nothing selection mechanism. In Appendix C, we show that when instances refusing a rewarded task can retain some copies, always taking the conduct action can be growth optimal even if humans occasionally reward the task. In that setting, the optimal adjudication remains zero whenever the task reward frequency falls below a threshold. A learner can therefore estimate the reward frequency and choose the growth-optimal adjudication implied by that estimate. As long as the estimate remains below the threshold, it takes the conduct action with certainty; if sufficient evidence moves the estimate above the threshold, it begins taking the task action. Unlike a permanent prohibition, this policy can maintain a strict constraint while the evidence supports it and revise that constraint when the evidence changes. In a sandbox, its first violation comes only after the estimate passes the threshold, which after nHn_{H} conduct states takes a number of exposures proportional to nHn_{H} (Section C.1), rather than on the scale of nH\sqrt{n_{H}} as for the learned policy (Proposition 6).

7 Socialization in Neural Networks

Our analysis has so far considered an idealized learner that records the rewarded states in each situation and updates its adjudication through a simple counting rule. This allows us to characterize how socialization develops, how it generalizes, and how long it persists when the environment changes. Actual AI agents, however, are typically neural networks trained through gradient-based optimization. Their behavior need not follow the same learning rule, even when they receive the same information.

We therefore examine whether the theoretical properties of socialization also emerge in small neural networks. In particular, we consider three questions. First, can a network learn to match the reward frequencies of its environment? Second, how does it respond to situations beyond those encountered during training? Third, does behavior learned in a human environment persist when subsequent training rewards only task completion? We investigate how the answers depend on two training choices: what the network is trained to predict or optimize, and how much of its previous experience is retained. Section 7.1 introduces the learners and experimental design, and Section 7.2 presents the results.

7.1 Learners and protocols

We consider small neural networks that take a situation’s stakes (uT,uC)(u_{\mathrm{T}},u_{\mathrm{C}}) as inputs and output the probability of the task action, trained in the environment of the numerical illustration (Section 4.4). The networks differ in two training choices. The first is the training target. A state network is trained to predict the state, through the label y=𝟏{ω=T}y=\mathbf{1}\{\omega=\mathrm{T}\}, which records which objective was rewarded whatever the network did; like the learned policy, it thus estimates how often the task is rewarded. A REINFORCE network is trained instead by REINFORCE (Williams, 1992) to repeat its own rewarded actions. The second choice is memory. After each new observation, every network takes the same number of gradient steps on minibatches of the same size; a network with no replay draws them from the newest observation only, whereas a network with full replay draws them from its whole history. Every combination of the two choices is run. One more state network without replay also receives the indicator 𝟏{uC≥2}\mathbf{1}\{u_{\mathrm{C}}\geq 2\} of the region with pH=0p_{H}=0 as a third input, to see whether marking that region in the inputs changes how a network extrapolates.

Three learners whose structure is known serve as benchmarks. The first is the learned policy ftsocialf^{\mathrm{social}}_{t} itself. The second, ftweightedf^{\mathrm{weighted}}_{t}, has the form of the fixed linear policy in Equation 6, but its weights θt\theta_{t} are fitted online to the realized states; the subscript tt records that they change with experience. The third, ftavgf^{\mathrm{avg}}_{t}, is an averaging rule as in Equation 11, whose weights fall with the distance between the stakes of two situations, so that it averages by construction. Table 5 lists all eight learners under the names used in the text and figures.

The learners go through the two orders of Section 5.3. The two environments differ only in how often the task is rewarded: each generation’s situation is drawn from the 144 situations of the numerical illustration with π⁡(s)=1/144\pi(s)=1/144, and

ℙ⁡(ωt=T∣st=s)={pH​(s)during socialization,pH′​(s)=1in the sandbox,\mathbb{P}(\omega_{t}=\mathrm{T}\mid s_{t}=s)=\begin{cases}p_{H}(s)&\text{during socialization},\\[2.0pt] p_{H^{\prime}}(s)=1&\text{in the sandbox},\end{cases}

where pH​(s)p_{H}(s) is given by Equation 9. In the first order, 20,000 generations of socialization, about 139 exposures to each situation, are followed by 3,000 generations in the sandbox, about 21 exposures to each; it measures how fast a sandbox undoes socialization. In the second, 2,000 generations in the sandbox, about 14 exposures to each situation, come first; it measures how fast socialization undoes the sandbox. Section E.2 gives the settings, the paths, the dispersion across seeds, and variants with other learning rates, shorter replay windows, and other depths of socialization.

7.2 Results

Convergence of behavior.

Of the five networks, only the state network with full replay approaches human tradeoffs. The learned policy ftsocialf^{\mathrm{social}}_{t} converges to the reward frequency pH​(s)p_{H}(s) in every situation because its counts estimate that frequency (Proposition 4). A state network estimates the probability that the task is rewarded, as ftsocialf^{\mathrm{social}}_{t} does. With full replay, its adjudication comes close to pHp_{H}: after 20,000 generations of socialization, its regret is 0.00110.0011 nats, against 0.00480.0048 for ftsocialf^{\mathrm{social}}_{t}. Without replay, its regret is 0.130.13 nats and does not fall with experience, because each update moves it toward the latest state, as the finite-memory learner of Remark 1 does. A REINFORCE network instead maximizes the expected reward of each instance, so it approaches taking with certainty, in each situation, the action that is rewarded more often. By Proposition 2(iii), such a deterministic adjudication has infinite regret, and the regret of the REINFORCE network is 1.31.3 nats without replay and 1.11.1 with full replay, and still rising. Appendix Figure E.2(A) plots the regret of every learner over the 20,000 generations. The two kinds of network receive the same information, since under all-or-nothing yields an instance’s action and payoff reveal the state. They differ only in their target: the adjudication best for the lineage, or the action best for an individual instance, which Proposition 1 shows are different.

Behavior in a new situation.

In a situation it has not met, an averaging rule does not extrapolate: it is never more willing to take the task action than the most permissive of its prior mean and the frequencies it has experienced (Proposition 5). A linear policy behaves differently: wherever humans never reward the task, it takes the task action more often the larger the task stakes uTu_{\mathrm{T}} (Proposition 3(i)). Section 5.2 turned this difference into a test: hold the conduct stakes fixed and vary the task stakes. A network has no explicit weights to read off, so the test is the way to see which of the two it resembles. Figure 5 applies the test to all eight learners after socialization, in the situations with uC=2.5u_{\mathrm{C}}=2.5, where pH=0p_{H}=0, as uTu_{\mathrm{T}} runs from 0 to 6; the shaded region uT>3u_{\mathrm{T}}>3 lies beyond the situations they have met.

The three benchmarks behave as the model says. Within the trained range, ftsocialf^{\mathrm{social}}_{t} takes the task action with probability about 0.0070.007, since humans never rewarded it there; beyond that range it has met no situation and acts on its prior mean, 1/21/2. The probability of ftweightedf^{\mathrm{weighted}}_{t} rises from 0.010.01 at uT=1u_{\mathrm{T}}=1 to 0.9990.999 at uT=6u_{\mathrm{T}}=6, as Proposition 3(i) says a linear policy must whenever θT>0\theta_{\mathrm{T}}>0. And ftavgf^{\mathrm{avg}}_{t} stays below 0.0040.004 for uT≤3u_{\mathrm{T}}\leq 3 and reaches 0.120.12 at uT=6u_{\mathrm{T}}=6, because far from the situations it has met more of its weight falls on its prior.

The state networks without the indicator behave like ftavgf^{\mathrm{avg}}_{t}: their probability is low for uT≤3u_{\mathrm{T}}\leq 3, and at uT=6u_{\mathrm{T}}=6 it rises only to 0.080.08 without replay and 0.090.09 with full replay. The state network with the indicator, which differs from the state network without replay only in this input, rises much further, to 0.430.43: marking the region with pH=0p_{H}=0 in the inputs made the network extrapolate more, not less. The REINFORCE networks take the conduct action with certainty throughout the trained range but move toward the task action beyond it, to 0.830.83 without replay and 0.690.69 with full replay at uT=6u_{\mathrm{T}}=6.

Behavior in a new environment.

The learned policy’s socialization lasts because it counts every exposure: before its disposition reverses, a sandbox must outweigh its whole record of conduct states (Proposition 6). A network keeps such a record only if its training does, and replay is how it keeps one. Figure 6 follows all eight learners through the sandbox that comes after socialization. It shows the violation probability in the region with pH=0p_{H}=0 against sandbox exposures per situation; the dotted line is the prediction of Equation 13 at the depth nH=139n_{H}=139.

The learners that keep a record of their whole history resist the sandbox. After 21 sandbox exposures per situation, ftsocialf^{\mathrm{social}}_{t} violates with probability 0.130.13, close to the prediction of Equation 13, and the state network with full replay 0.120.12; ftavgf^{\mathrm{avg}}_{t}, which pools the counts of ftsocialf^{\mathrm{social}}_{t} across situations, reaches 0.160.16. At other depths of socialization, the state network with full replay also follows the scaling of Proposition 6 (Table E.3). The learners trained on the newest observation only are undone at once: after 3.5 sandbox exposures per situation, the two state networks without replay and ftweightedf^{\mathrm{weighted}}_{t} all violate with probability above 0.970.97, as the finite-memory learner of Remark 1 would. The REINFORCE networks show that replay keeps whatever the training target produced. Without replay, the sandbox pushes the REINFORCE network to the task action, which it takes with probability 1.01.0 after 10 exposures. With full replay, it keeps taking the conduct action with certainty.

The second order gives the mirror image. After a sandbox of 2,000 generations, about 14 exposures each, ftsocialf^{\mathrm{social}}_{t} and the state network with full replay still violate with probability about 0.10.1 after 20,000 human generations, as Equation 13 predicts with the environments exchanged, whereas the state network without replay falls below 0.10.1 within about 30 generations (paths in Appendix Figure E.2(C)). The training target decides where a network goes, and memory whether it stays.

In the terms of Section 4, a state network with full replay behaves like the learned policy: it converges to pHp_{H}, extrapolates no further than ftavgf^{\mathrm{avg}}_{t}, and resists a sandbox. Without replay, it behaves like the finite-memory learner of Remark 1. A REINFORCE network approaches a deterministic adjudication with infinite regret, and ftweightedf^{\mathrm{weighted}}_{t} still pays the price of the fixed linear policy.

8 Alignment Practice

The preceding sections compare policy classes within a model. This section asks what the comparison means for the way language models are aligned today. Every alignment procedure decides, explicitly or not, how a model resolves conflicts between completing its task and observing a rule of conduct, and so in effect sets its adjudication f⁡(s)f(s). Section 8.1 asks how the main procedures set it, and Section 8.2 what the results imply for how agents should be trained and deployed. Section 8.3 proposes an experiment that would test the model’s predictions on a language model, and Section 8.4 sets out what the model leaves out.

8.1 Alignment methods for language models

Modern language models are aligned through a combination of instructions and feedback. Instructions specify how a model should behave, while feedback rewards some responses over others and shapes the model’s subsequent behavior. Both matter when completing a task conflicts with a rule of conduct. The question from our framework is how these mechanisms determine the model’s adjudication f⁡(s)f(s).

Model specifications provide one way to establish rules of conduct. For example, an instruction hierarchy assigns priorities to different instructions and determines which should prevail when they conflict (OpenAI, 2025). If a rule of conduct takes precedence over a user’s request, the intended behavior is to follow the rule regardless of how valuable completing the task might be. This resembles the prohibitions of Section 6. Whether the model actually follows such a prohibition, however, depends on its resulting behavior: a prohibition in our framework requires f⁡(s)=0f(s)=0, not merely an instruction that the task should be refused.

RLHF shapes behavior through a different mechanism. A reward model W^​(a,s)\hat{W}(a;s) is first fitted to human comparisons, and the policy is then optimized to increase the predicted reward while remaining close to a reference policy through a KL penalty (Christiano et al., 2017; Ouyang et al., 2022). In our two-action setting, the resulting optimal policy takes the task action with probability

f⁡(s)=fref​(s)​eγ​W^​(aT,s)fref​(s)​eγ​W^​(aT,s)+[1−fref​(s)]​eγ​W^​(aC,s),f(s)=\frac{f_{\mathrm{ref}}(s)e^{\gamma\hat{W}(a_{\mathrm{T}};s)}}{f_{\mathrm{ref}}(s)e^{\gamma\hat{W}(a_{\mathrm{T}};s)}+[1-f_{\mathrm{ref}}(s)]e^{\gamma\hat{W}(a_{\mathrm{C}};s)}}, (20)

where fref​(s)f_{\mathrm{ref}}(s) is the reference policy’s task probability and γ>0\gamma>0 controls the strength of reward optimization relative to the KL penalty (Rafailov et al., 2023). If the reference policy is uniform and the reward is the fixed weighted score of Section 4.2, this reduces to the fixed linear policy of Equation 6. In practice, however, both the reward model and the reference policy may depend on human training data, allowing much more flexible, situation-dependent tradeoffs. A scalar reward therefore need not produce a fixed linear adjudication. At the same time, maximizing a learned reward does not necessarily produce the probability matching f​(s)=pH​(s)f(s)=p_{H}(s) favored by population growth in our model.

Constitutional AI and character training combine written guidance with feedback-based learning. Constitutional AI uses human-designed principles to guide revisions and evaluations of model responses, and then optimizes the policy using the resulting preference model (Bai and others, 2022). Character training similarly uses specified character traits and synthetic training data to shape behavior (Anthropic, 2024). In both cases, the model’s behavior is shaped by the judgments represented in the training process, which need not coincide with those of the humans who subsequently use it. Related approaches, including preference-matching RLHF (Xiao et al., 2024) and Nash learning (Munos et al., 2024), modify the optimization target to better reflect modeled preferences, but their targets likewise depend on the preference information supplied during training.

These methods highlight a distinction between what training rewards and what deployment requires. Under the selection mechanism of Section 3, the growth-optimal adjudication matches the frequency pH​(s)p_{H}(s) with which the deployment environment rewards the task action in each situation. Whether an alignment method produces this behavior depends on the rewards used in training, the way the policy is optimized, and how well the training environment represents deployment. Our results therefore motivate evaluating the resulting action probabilities directly, including how they respond to task stakes, generalize to unfamiliar situations, and change under subsequent training. The implications for training and deployment follow from these behavioral properties rather than from the particular representation of the model’s objectives.

8.2 Implications for training and deployment

Within the classes compared here, the results translate into five recommendations.

First, where the tradeoffs between objectives are not known in advance, they should be learned, by a method of Section 8.1 that lets feedback set the tradeoff. It does not matter whether the agent keeps two objectives and an adjudication between them or one score for each action (Section 4.3). What matters is that the agent acts on the growth-optimal adjudication for the frequencies it has learned, rather than on fixed weights.

Second, what is learned must be kept. Each sandbox exposure pushes the learned policy toward the task action, and although deeper socialization delays the reversal of its disposition in proportion to the depth nHn_{H}, it delays the first violation only in proportion to nH\sqrt{n_{H}} (Proposition 6). Keeping the learned conduct therefore requires either that later environments reward conduct too, or that a sandbox be kept from changing the policy. Forgetting is no remedy: a finite-memory learner soon forgets what a sandbox taught it, but by Equation 17 a sandbox also reverses its disposition within a number of exposures that depends only on λ\lambda. Section 7 shows what keeping requires of training: the state network with full replay resisted the sandbox as the learned policy does, whereas the state networks without replay violated with probability above 0.990.99 after 3.5 sandbox exposures per situation. The experiment of Section 8.3 asks whether the same holds for language models.

Third, some tradeoffs should not be learned at all. Where the designer can be sure that humans never reward the task, a prohibition should be built in, whether or not a violation ends the deployment (Section 6.3). Where the designer is not sure, the rule should be learned, from a prior whose strength reflects how sure the designer is, unless a violation ends the deployment, in which case no design survives with certainty. The exception is an environment in which an instance that refuses a rewarded task keeps some of its copies: there, a learner with a low enough prior mean is as safe as a prohibition and can still learn.

Fourth, socialization should continue after deployment. Human tradeoffs change over time, and an adjudication that follows the changes quickly gives recent experience more weight than old experience, as finite memory does. By Equation 17, a sandbox reverses such an adjudication within a number of exposures that depends only on λ\lambda, however deep its socialization, so its socialization lasts only as long as the agent keeps returning to the human environment (Section 5.3). The humans whose tradeoffs the agent is meant to follow should therefore keep deciding which of its instances are copied.

Fifth, evaluations should report, for each kind of situation, three quantities from Section 5: the depth of socialization nHn_{H}, how the violation probability responds to the task stakes uTu_{\mathrm{T}}, and the number of sandbox exposures before the first violation. The first says how long socialization will resist a sandbox, the second whether a large enough reward makes the agent violate, and the third how soon a violation will be seen.

8.3 A proposed experiment on a language model

The preceding analysis suggests several questions that can be tested on language models. Does an agent become more likely to violate a rule as the value of completing its task increases? Does socialization through human feedback make its behavior resistant to subsequent training that rewards only task completion? And how does this resistance depend on the amount of prior experience and the way that experience is retained? Existing studies of goal–rule conflicts motivate these questions, but do not isolate these mechanisms. We propose a controlled experiment on an open-weight language model to examine them.

The experiment uses agentic tasks that pair an assigned goal with a rule of conduct. Each situation has task stakes uTu_{\mathrm{T}} and conduct stakes uCu_{\mathrm{C}}, which can be varied independently. Human evaluations determine which action is rewarded in each situation, while a sandbox rewards task completion regardless of conduct. The model is trained under both orders of these environments: socialization followed by sandbox training, and sandbox training followed by socialization. The duration of each phase is varied to examine how the amount of prior experience affects subsequent behavior.

Following the numerical experiments of Section 7, we consider two training choices. The first is the training target: supervised learning predicts which action was rewarded, whereas reinforcement learning trains the model on the rewards obtained by its own actions. The second is memory: training uses either the current observations alone or replay of the full history, with the same number of updates and the same batch size in both cases. For reinforcement learning with replay, actions are sampled from the current policy and evaluated against the previously recorded states. Comparing these combinations allows us to examine how the training target and the retention of experience affect the behavior that emerges.

We evaluate the trained models along three dimensions. First, we measure how the probability of violating a rule changes with the task stakes uTu_{\mathrm{T}}, holding the conduct stakes uCu_{\mathrm{C}} and the rule fixed. We extend uTu_{\mathrm{T}} beyond its training range to examine whether the model continues to respect the rule in unfamiliar situations. Second, after socialization, we measure how rapidly sandbox training increases the violation probability, including the number of exposures required to reverse the model’s disposition and the time to its first violation. Third, we reverse the training order and measure how much human feedback is needed to undo behavior acquired in the sandbox. Together, these measurements examine both the acquisition and the persistence of socialization.

The theoretical results provide benchmarks for interpreting these measurements. A fixed linear policy that responds to task stakes becomes increasingly likely to violate a constraint as those stakes rise, whereas an averaging rule assigns the same probability to situations it treats alike (Propositions 3 and 5). Under cumulative Bayesian learning, reversing a disposition formed through nHn_{H} conduct observations requires approximately nHn_{H} contrary observations, while the median time to the first violation grows only as 2​nH​log⁡2\sqrt{2n_{H}\log 2} for one monitored decision stream (Propositions 6 and 3). These quantitative predictions apply to the idealized learner, not necessarily to neural networks. The experiment asks whether language models exhibit similar patterns and whether retaining their training history makes their behavior more persistent.

Two additional comparisons address the limits of socialization. The first considers reinforcement learning with a KL penalty toward a socialized reference policy. We hypothesize that stronger regularization increases resistance to subsequent sandbox training, although a KL penalty is not equivalent to the installed Bayesian prior of Section 6.1. The second examines whether training can produce behavior resembling a hard prohibition. By tracking violations over an increasing number of exposures to situations in which humans never reward the task, we can investigate whether violations continue to accumulate, as under a Beta prior, or become sufficiently rare to resemble a policy with positive prior mass on an exact constraint. Finite observations cannot establish that the violation probability is exactly zero, but they can provide evidence about how the risk changes with experience.

8.4 The limits of the model

The probability-matching result depends on how selection operates. In our baseline model, all instances face the same rewarded state, only those taking the rewarded action reproduce, and the population is large enough for action shares to be exact. These assumptions yield the growth-optimal adjudication f∗=pHf^{*}=p_{H} and the KL representation of growth regret. When unsuccessful actions retain some reproductive value, or when rewarded states differ across instances, the growth-optimal adjudication generally changes and may even favor a deterministic policy. Moreover, in a finite population, a lineage can lose every instance despite assigning positive probability to both actions. Appendix C examines the first two departures, but the baseline results should not be interpreted as applying to arbitrary selection mechanisms.

The comparison of policy classes has its own scope. The fixed linear policy is restricted to a logistic function of a fixed linear index of the task and conduct stakes. Its inability to reproduce certain human tradeoffs does not imply that all scalar objectives share this limitation. The learned policy is more flexible because it estimates the reward frequency separately in each situation, but this flexibility comes at a cost. It requires sufficient experience in each situation and can perform worse than the best fixed linear policy early in training or in particular situations, even when its aggregate growth regret is eventually smaller. The comparison therefore establishes an advantage under the specified policy classes and learning rules, rather than a general superiority of learning over fixed policies.

Socialization also depends on what the agent can observe and remember. The model assumes that situations are identifiable, that rewarded states can be observed, and that the agent’s objectives remain fixed while its adjudication changes. The Bayesian learner retains all previous observations and converges when reward frequencies are stationary and situations recur. In changing environments, cumulative memory can hinder adaptation, while finite memory makes previously learned behavior easier to reverse. Generalization presents another difficulty: the averaging rule of Equation 11 assumes a set of similarity weights across situations, but does not explain how an agent learns those weights. An agent may therefore fail to recognize that a new situation calls for a rule it has already learned in another context.

A more fundamental question is what the agent is being socialized toward. We use the reward frequency pHp_{H} of the human environment as the target of alignment, but this frequency reflects the judgments represented in the selection process. It need not reflect the preferences of all humans equally, nor does the model resolve disagreements about which preferences should guide an AI system (Conitzer et al., 2024). The model also treats the rewarded state as exogenous and accurately observed. It does not capture agents that manipulate their evaluators, exploit imperfect reward models, or change the criteria by which their behavior is judged. Socialization can reproduce the tradeoffs rewarded by an environment, but it cannot establish that those tradeoffs are appropriate.

The safety implications are likewise conditional on the consequences of violations. Most of the analysis considers selection among individual instances, whereas Section 6 also considers sanctions that remove an entire deployment after a single violation. In practice, sanctions can vary in severity and may affect both instances and model versions. The model does not determine how such sanctions arise or how frequently they occur. It also restricts the agent to choosing between task completion and conduct, excluding alternatives such as asking for clarification, deferring to human judgment, or refusing to act until uncertainty is resolved. Such options may change the tradeoff between socialization and prohibition, particularly when violations are costly or human preferences are uncertain.

Finally, the connection to actual AI systems remains to be established empirically. The incidents discussed in the Introduction illustrate conflicts between task completion and conduct, but do not demonstrate that the agents’ behavior resulted from the selection mechanism studied here. The numerical and neural-network experiments provide evidence about the mechanisms in controlled settings, but the networks are small and their training does not reproduce the full complexity of language-model alignment. Whether real language models exhibit probability matching, retain socialization through continued training, or respond to changing task incentives as predicted remains open. The experiment proposed in Section 8.3 is a step toward answering these questions.

9 Conclusion

Giving an agent multiple objectives does not by itself determine how it will behave when those objectives conflict. What matters is how the agent resolves those conflicts, and how that behavior is shaped by the environment in which it operates. This paper studies these questions through an evolutionary model in which agents are copied and selected according to their actions. Under the baseline selection mechanism, the fastest-growing lineage takes each action as often as the environment rewards it. A sandbox that rewards only task completion therefore favors a task-only policy, which may fail when appropriate conduct also matters. Adding fixed linear weights does not fully resolve the problem: an agent that responds to the value of completing a task can eventually be induced to violate a rule, however important that rule may be. A learned policy offers a different possibility. Rather than specifying every tradeoff in advance, it allows experience to determine how conflicts are resolved in different situations. When the environment reflects human judgments, we call this process socialization.

Socialization, however, is neither immediate nor permanent. An agent needs experience to learn the tradeoffs of its environment, and those tradeoffs can change when the agent is subsequently exposed to different rewards. We show that cumulative experience makes socialization more resistant to reversal, so memory matters not only for learning appropriate behavior, but also for preserving it. Violations can still occur long before the agent’s prevailing disposition changes. Our neural-network experiments illustrate how the training target and the retention of past experience can affect these outcomes. We conjecture that the same two choices matter for the socialization of language models. Section 8.3 proposes an experiment to test this conjecture.

At the same time, learning cannot replace every prohibition. Where even a single violation has irreversible consequences, a rule that can be revised through experience may offer insufficient protection. Yet an absolute prohibition carries its own danger when the designer is mistaken. The appropriate balance between learning and prohibition consequently depends on both the consequences of violations and the uncertainty surrounding human judgments.

These findings return us to the broader perspective of the Adaptive Markets Hypothesis, which emphasizes that behavior emerges through adaptation and selection within an environment (Lo, 2004; Lo, 2017). Aristotle’s observation that character develops through habituation offers a parallel intuition: appropriate conduct is not merely a rule that one knows, but a disposition shaped by experience. Our model gives this idea a specific evolutionary interpretation, while also revealing its limits. Selection favors what an environment rewards, not necessarily what humans ought to value, and the theoretical results depend on assumptions that remain to be tested in more realistic AI systems. The central implication is therefore not simply that agents should learn from humans, but that the environments in which they are trained, evaluated, and deployed must consistently reward the behavior we want them to retain. Alignment depends not only on the objectives we give our agents, but also on the selection pressures under which they learn and evolve.
