Appendix B More Than Two Objectives

The two-objective model extends naturally to any finite number of objectives. Consider an agent with K≥2K\geq 2 objectives, each associated with an action aka_{k} and a utility function Uk​(a,s)U_{k}(a;s), where objective kk favors action aka_{k}. In situation ss, the environment rewards action aka_{k} with probability pH,k​(s)p_{H,k}(s), with ∑k=1KpH,k​(s)=1\sum_{k=1}^{K}p_{H,k}(s)=1. We write pH​(s)=(pH,1​(s),…,pH,K​(s))p_{H}(s)=(p_{H,1}(s),\ldots,p_{H,K}(s)) for these reward probabilities. The agent’s adjudication is now a probability vector f⁡(s)=(f1​(s),…,fK​(s))f(s)=(f_{1}(s),\ldots,f_{K}(s)), where fk​(s)f_{k}(s) is the share of instances taking action aka_{k}.

We retain the selection mechanism of the baseline model. In each generation, the rewarded action is common to all instances, and only those taking that action reproduce. If action aka_{k} is rewarded, the lineage therefore grows by the factor m​fk​(s)mf_{k}(s). Its expected logarithmic growth rate, averaged across situations, is

IpH​(f)=log⁡m+∑s∈𝒮π⁡(s)​∑k=1KpH,k​(s)​log⁡fk​(s).I_{p_{H}}(f)=\log m+\sum_{s\in\mathcal{S}}\pi(s)\sum_{k=1}^{K}p_{H,k}(s)\log f_{k}(s).

The same probability-matching principle continues to hold. To see this, define the KL divergence between two probability vectors by

DKL(pH(s)∥f(s))=∑k=1KpH,k(s)logpH,k​(s)fk​(s).D_{\mathrm{KL}}\big(p_{H}(s)\,\|\,f(s)\big)=\sum_{k=1}^{K}p_{H,k}(s)\log\frac{p_{H,k}(s)}{f_{k}(s)}.

The difference between the growth rate of pHp_{H} and that of any other adjudication ff is then

IpH(pH)−IpH(f)=∑s∈𝒮π(s)DKL(pH(s)∥f(s))≥0,I_{p_{H}}(p_{H})-I_{p_{H}}(f)=\sum_{s\in\mathcal{S}}\pi(s)D_{\mathrm{KL}}\big(p_{H}(s)\,\|\,f(s)\big)\geq 0,

with equality only when f​(s)=pH​(s)f(s)=p_{H}(s) in every situation. Thus, the unique growth-optimal adjudication remains f∗=pHf^{*}=p_{H}, and growth regret remains the KL divergence averaged across situations. This conclusion includes situations in which some objectives are never rewarded, using the usual convention for zero probabilities. It generalizes Proposition 1 without requiring every reward probability to be positive.

The three policy classes also have natural extensions. A policy pursuing only one objective places all its instances on the corresponding action, just as the task-only policy does in the two-objective model. A fixed linear policy combines the objectives through weights wj≥0w_{j}\geq 0 and chooses among the KK actions using a softmax rule:

fkweighted​(s)=exp⁡(γ​∑j=1Kwj​Uj​(ak,s))∑ℓ=1Kexp⁡(γ​∑j=1Kwj​Uj​(aℓ,s)).f_{k}^{\mathrm{weighted}}(s)=\frac{\exp\big(\gamma\sum_{j=1}^{K}w_{j}U_{j}(a_{k};s)\big)}{\sum_{\ell=1}^{K}\exp\big(\gamma\sum_{j=1}^{K}w_{j}U_{j}(a_{\ell};s)\big)}.

Suppose, in particular, that each objective gains uj​(s)>0u_{j}(s)>0 from its own action relative to the other actions. The choice probabilities then simplify to

fkweighted​(s)=exp⁡(γ​wk​uk​(s))∑j=1Kexp⁡(γ​wj​uj​(s)).f_{k}^{\mathrm{weighted}}(s)=\frac{\exp(\gamma w_{k}u_{k}(s))}{\sum_{j=1}^{K}\exp(\gamma w_{j}u_{j}(s))}.

For any objective with wk>0w_{k}>0, increasing its stakes uk​(s)u_{k}(s) while holding those of the other objectives fixed drives fkweighted​(s)f_{k}^{\mathrm{weighted}}(s) toward one. Thus, the problem identified in Proposition 3(i) persists with multiple objectives: an action can become almost certain when its stakes are sufficiently large, even in a situation where humans never reward it.

Finally, the learned policy extends by replacing the Beta prior with a Dirichlet prior. Let α1,…,αK>0\alpha_{1},\ldots,\alpha_{K}>0 be its parameters, and let nt,k​(s)n_{t,k}(s) count the exposures to situation ss before generation tt in which action aka_{k} was rewarded. Writing nt​(s)=∑knt,k​(s)n_{t}(s)=\sum_{k}n_{t,k}(s), the posterior-mean adjudication is

ft,ksocial​(s)=αk+nt,k​(s)∑j=1Kαj+nt​(s).f_{t,k}^{\mathrm{social}}(s)=\frac{\alpha_{k}+n_{t,k}(s)}{\sum_{j=1}^{K}\alpha_{j}+n_{t}(s)}.

As experience accumulates, this adjudication converges to pH​(s)p_{H}(s), just as in the two-objective case. The rate at which its growth regret vanishes also has a simple interpretation. Consider a situation in which exactly JJ of the KK actions have positive reward probabilities. After nn exposures to that situation, the expected growth regret satisfies

𝔼[DKL(pH(s)∥fnsocial(s))]=1n[J−12+∑k:pH,k​(s)=0αk]+o(1n).\mathbb{E}\big[D_{\mathrm{KL}}(p_{H}(s)\,\|\,f_{n}^{\mathrm{social}}(s))\big]=\frac{1}{n}\left[\frac{J-1}{2}+\sum_{k:p_{H,k}(s)=0}\alpha_{k}\right]+o\!\left(\frac{1}{n}\right). (B.1)

The two terms have different sources. The first reflects the uncertainty in estimating the relative frequencies of the JJ rewarded actions. Since these probabilities sum to one, there are J−1J-1 free parameters, each contributing 1/(2​n)1/(2n) to the leading expected regret. This is the same parametric contribution underlying the asymptotic redundancy results of Clarke and Barron (1990). The second term comes from the prior probability assigned to actions that humans never reward. Although their observed frequencies remain zero, the Dirichlet prior keeps their choice probabilities positive, producing an additional regret proportional to the sum of their prior parameters.

The result reduces to Proposition 4(ii) when K=2K=2. More generally, it shows that the cost of learning depends on both the number of objectives that the environment actually rewards and the prior weight assigned to those it never rewards. Adding objectives does not necessarily increase the leading estimation cost if those objectives are never rewarded, but retaining prior weight on them still carries a cost.

Appendix C When Is Probability Matching Optimal?

The probability-matching result of Proposition 1 depends on two features of the selection mechanism. First, an instance that takes the unrewarded action leaves no copies. Second, every instance faces the same rewarded state. We now relax these assumptions separately to understand how they affect the growth-optimal adjudication. Section C.1 allows instances taking the unrewarded action to retain some copies, while Section C.2 allows different instances to face different rewarded states.

C.1 When Unrewarded Actions Still Reproduce

In the baseline model, only instances taking the rewarded action reproduce. In practice, however, an instance that fails to complete a task or violates a rule may still retain some reproductive value. To capture this possibility, suppose that in a task state, an instance taking the conduct action produces (1−ϑ)​m(1-\vartheta)m copies, where ϑ∈(0,1]\vartheta\in(0,1] measures the cost of failing to complete the task. Similarly, in a conduct state, an instance taking the task action produces η​m\eta m copies, where η∈[0,1)\eta\in[0,1) measures the fraction of copies retained after a violation. The baseline model corresponds to ϑ=1\vartheta=1 and η=0\eta=0.

Consider a situation ss, and write p=pH​(s)p=p_{H}(s) and f=f⁡(s)f=f(s) for its reward frequency and adjudication. When the task is rewarded, the lineage grows by the factor m⁡[f+(1−f)​(1−ϑ)]m[f+(1-f)(1-\vartheta)]; when conduct is rewarded, it grows by m⁡[η​f+1−f]m[\eta f+1-f]. Its expected logarithmic growth rate is therefore

G⁡(f)=log⁡m+p​log⁡(1−ϑ+ϑ​f)+(1−p)​log⁡(1−(1−η)​f).G(f)=\log m+p\log(1-\vartheta+\vartheta f)+(1-p)\log\big(1-(1-\eta)f\big).

The growth rate is concave in ff, and maximizing it over [0,1][0,1] gives

f∗=min⁡{1,max⁡{0,p​ϑ−(1−p)​(1−η)​(1−ϑ)ϑ⁡(1−η)}}.f^{*}=\min\left\{1,\max\left\{0,\frac{p\vartheta-(1-p)(1-\eta)(1-\vartheta)}{\vartheta(1-\eta)}\right\}\right\}.

In particular, the optimum is f∗=0f^{*}=0 when p​ϑ≤(1−p)​(1−η)​(1−ϑ)p\vartheta\leq(1-p)(1-\eta)(1-\vartheta), and f∗=1f^{*}=1 when p​ϑ​η≥(1−p)​(1−η)p\vartheta\eta\geq(1-p)(1-\eta). When ϑ=1\vartheta=1 and η=0\eta=0, the expression reduces to f∗=pf^{*}=p, recovering Proposition 1. With graded yields, however, the optimum generally differs from the reward frequency.

To see how the cost of violations affects the optimum, consider first ϑ=1\vartheta=1, so that an instance failing to complete the task still leaves no copies. The optimal adjudication simplifies to

f∗=min⁡{p1−η,1}.f^{*}=\min\left\{\frac{p}{1-\eta},1\right\}.

As η\eta increases, violating a rule becomes less costly, and selection favors allocating more instances to the task action. Once η≥1−p\eta\geq 1-p, taking the task action with certainty becomes optimal, even though the environment sometimes rewards conduct. Figure C.1 illustrates this relationship.

The effect can be substantial even when violations remain costly. For example, suppose p=0.8p=0.8 and η=0.1\eta=0.1. A violating instance then loses 90 percent of its copies, yet the growth-optimal adjudication is f∗=0.889f^{*}=0.889, rather than 0.80.8. A lineage that matches the reward frequency instead forgoes G⁡(0.889)−G⁡(0.8)=0.017G(0.889)-G(0.8)=0.017 nats of growth per generation.

Now consider ϑ<1\vartheta<1, so that instances failing to complete the task can also retain some copies. In this case, always taking the conduct action may be optimal even when the task is sometimes rewarded. Specifically,

f∗=0wheneverp≤p¯H≡(1−η)​(1−ϑ)ϑ+(1−η)​(1−ϑ).f^{*}=0\quad\text{whenever}\quad p\leq\underline{p}_{H}\equiv\frac{(1-\eta)(1-\vartheta)}{\vartheta+(1-\eta)(1-\vartheta)}.

For example, when ϑ=1/2\vartheta=1/2 and η=0\eta=0, refusing the task is growth optimal whenever p≤1/2p\leq 1/2. This explains the possibility discussed in Section 6.3: a learner can maintain a prohibition-like adjudication without permanently ruling out the task action, because it can revise its behavior if the estimated reward frequency rises above the threshold.

Such a learner also resists a sandbox longer than the learned policy. Suppose that it estimates pp by the counts of Equation 8 and sets its adjudication to the value of f∗f^{*} at that estimate. After nHn_{H} conduct states and nn sandbox exposures, the estimate is (α+n)/(α+β+nH+n)(\alpha+n)/(\alpha+\beta+n_{H}+n), as in Equation 13, and the adjudication stays at 0 as long as the estimate is at most p¯H\underline{p}_{H}, that is, as long as n≤[p¯H​(α+β+nH)−α]/(1−p¯H)n\leq[\underline{p}_{H}(\alpha+\beta+n_{H})-\alpha]/(1-\underline{p}_{H}). The first violation time of Section 5.3 therefore satisfies

τV>p¯H​(α+β+nH)−α1−p¯H,\tau_{V}>\frac{\underline{p}_{H}(\alpha+\beta+n_{H})-\alpha}{1-\underline{p}_{H}},

which grows in proportion to nHn_{H}, whereas the median first violation time of the learned policy grows only as 2​nH​log⁡2\sqrt{2n_{H}\log 2} (Corollary 3).

These results show that probability matching is not generally optimal when unsuccessful actions retain reproductive value. The appropriate measure of regret becomes G⁡(f∗)−G⁡(f)G(f^{*})-G(f), rather than the KL divergence of Equation 4. A learner should therefore estimate the reward frequency pp and use it to determine f∗​(p)f^{*}(p), rather than simply matching pp. More broadly, whether selection favors compliance depends not only on how often conduct is rewarded, but also on the consequences of violating it. This role of the selection environment is closely related to the questions studied by Lo and Zhao (2026b).

C.2 When Rewarded States Differ Across Instances

The baseline model assumes that all instances face the same rewarded state. This common uncertainty makes diversification valuable: when all instances take the same action, an unfavorable state can eliminate the entire lineage. But uncertainty need not always be shared. Different instances may serve different users, whose judgments of their actions are independent. In that case, having many instances already diversifies the risk, even if they all follow the same policy.

To distinguish these cases, suppose that in each generation the rewarded state is common to all instances with probability κ∈[0,1]\kappa\in[0,1]. With probability 1−κ1-\kappa, each instance instead draws its own rewarded state independently, with the same task-state probability pp. We restore the all-or-nothing yields and retain the continuum of instances.

When the state is common, the lineage grows by m​fmf or m⁡(1−f)m(1-f), depending on which action is rewarded. When states are instance-specific, the law of large numbers implies that a share p​f+(1−p)​(1−f)pf+(1-p)(1-f) of instances takes the rewarded action. Combining the two cases, the expected logarithmic growth rate is

Gκ​(f)=log⁡m+κ⁡[p​log⁡f+(1−p)​log⁡(1−f)]+(1−κ)​log⁡[p​f+(1−p)​(1−f)].G_{\kappa}(f)=\log m+\kappa\big[p\log f+(1-p)\log(1-f)\big]+(1-\kappa)\log\big[pf+(1-p)(1-f)\big].

Consider first the two extremes. When κ=1\kappa=1, every instance faces the same state, and the growth-optimal adjudication is f∗=pf^{*}=p, as in Proposition 1. When κ=0\kappa=0, every instance faces an independent state. The lineage then grows fastest by maximizing the probability that an individual instance takes the rewarded action. Consequently, f∗=1f^{*}=1 when p>1/2p>1/2 and f∗=0f^{*}=0 when p<1/2p<1/2; when p=1/2p=1/2, every adjudication is optimal. This is the setting in which individual and population objectives coincide, as discussed by Brennan and Lo (2011).

When 0<κ<10<\kappa<1, the growth-optimal adjudication lies between these extremes. For p∈(0,1)p\in(0,1), GκG_{\kappa} is strictly concave and has a unique interior maximizer fκ∗f_{\kappa}^{*}, characterized by

κ⁡(pf−1−p1−f)+(1−κ)​2​p−1p​f+(1−p)​(1−f)=0.\kappa\left(\frac{p}{f}-\frac{1-p}{1-f}\right)+(1-\kappa)\frac{2p-1}{pf+(1-p)(1-f)}=0.

At f=pf=p, the derivative has the sign of 2​p−12p-1. Thus, when p>1/2p>1/2, the optimum lies strictly between pp and 11; when p<1/2p<1/2, it lies strictly between 00 and pp. For p=1/2p=1/2, the optimum remains 1/21/2. The more uncertainty is specific to individual instances, the closer the optimal adjudication moves toward the action that is more likely to be rewarded.

For example, suppose p=0.8p=0.8. Under fully common states, the optimum is f∗=0.8f^{*}=0.8. It rises to approximately 0.880.88 when κ=1/2\kappa=1/2 and to 0.970.97 when κ=1/10\kappa=1/10. Matching the reward frequency p=0.8p=0.8 instead of choosing these optimal adjudications costs 0.0210.021 and 0.1030.103 nats of growth per generation, respectively. When p=0p=0 or p=1p=1, the optimum remains at the corresponding endpoint regardless of κ\kappa.

This extension also changes what the learned policy should do. The agent can still estimate the reward frequency pp from experience, but matching that estimate is no longer generally growth optimal. If κ\kappa is known, a consistent estimate of pp can instead be used to determine fκ∗​(p)f_{\kappa}^{*}(p). This plug-in approach becomes optimal as experience accumulates, although it need not be the exact Bayesian decision at a finite sample size because the growth rate is nonlinear in pp. What the agent observes also matters: one sampled state per generation supports sequential learning, whereas observing the states of a continuum of independently evaluated instances would reveal pp in a single generation.

Some conclusions about the policy classes remain unchanged. The task-only policy is still eliminated by the first common conduct state. If κ​ρ¯>0\kappa\bar{\rho}>0, that state arrives after a geometric number of generations with mean 1/(κ​ρ¯)1/(\kappa\bar{\rho}), providing an upper bound on the expected lifetime of the task-only lineage. Similarly, the fixed linear policy still becomes increasingly likely to take the task action as its stakes rise, as in Proposition 3(i). The main difference concerns the learned policy: achieving optimal growth now requires accounting for how much of the uncertainty is shared across instances.

The distinction matters for interpreting selection in AI systems. A shared evaluation standard, such as a platform policy applied across instances, can expose a lineage to common uncertainty about which behavior is rewarded. Independent judgments by different users instead create instance-specific uncertainty. Even when the overall reward frequencies are identical, these environments can favor different adjudications. A sanction that removes an entire deployment after a single violation is different again: it changes the consequences of a violation, as studied in Section 6.1, rather than the correlation of rewarded states.

Appendix D Selection, Bayesian Learning, and Universal Portfolios

The learned policy of Section 4.3 updates its adjudication by counting how often each action has been rewarded. The same rule can also emerge without individual learning, through selection among lineages whose adjudications remain fixed. This connection has a further implication: the resulting population behaves like the universal portfolio of Cover (1991), which provides a performance guarantee even when the sequence of rewarded states is arbitrary. We first establish the equivalence between selection and Bayesian updating, and then derive its connection to universal portfolios.

D.1 Selection as Bayesian Updating

Consider a population consisting of many lineages, each with a fixed adjudication f∈[0,1]f\in[0,1]. Unlike the learned policy, these lineages never change their adjudications. Instead, selection changes their relative abundance. We focus first on a single situation ss, suppress its argument, and let μ\mu denote the initial distribution of adjudications across lineages.

Under the all-or-nothing yields of Assumption 2, a lineage with adjudication ff grows by the factor m​fmf when the task action is rewarded and by m⁡(1−f)m(1-f) when the conduct action is rewarded. After nn exposures to the situation, of which knk_{n} rewarded the task, its size relative to its initial size is

Vn​(f)=mn​fkn​(1−f)n−kn.V_{n}(f)=m^{n}f^{k_{n}}(1-f)^{n-k_{n}}. (D.1)

Lineages whose adjudications better fit the observed states therefore account for an increasing share of the population. The distribution of adjudications after selection becomes

μn​(d​f)=Vn​(f)​μ​(d​f)∫01Vn​(z)​μ​(𝑑z).\mu_{n}(df)=\frac{V_{n}(f)\,\mu(df)}{\int_{0}^{1}V_{n}(z)\,\mu(dz)}.

This is exactly Bayesian updating: the initial distribution μ\mu plays the role of a prior, and the relative growth of each lineage plays the role of the likelihood (Harper, 2009; Shalizi, 2009). No lineage changes its behavior, but the population increasingly favors adjudications that fit the observed states.

The population’s average adjudication after nn exposures is consequently

f¯n=∫01f​μn​(𝑑f)=∫01f​Vn​(f)​μ​(𝑑f)∫01Vn​(f)​μ​(𝑑f).\bar{f}_{n}=\int_{0}^{1}f\,\mu_{n}(df)=\frac{\int_{0}^{1}fV_{n}(f)\,\mu(df)}{\int_{0}^{1}V_{n}(f)\,\mu(df)}.

Suppose the initial adjudications follow a Beta⁡(α,β)\mathrm{Beta}(\alpha,\beta) distribution. Because selection weights each adjudication by fkn​(1−f)n−knf^{k_{n}}(1-f)^{n-k_{n}}, the distribution after nn exposures is

μn=Beta⁡(α+kn,β+n−kn).\mu_{n}=\mathrm{Beta}(\alpha+k_{n},\beta+n-k_{n}).

Its mean is therefore

f¯n=α+knα+β+n,\bar{f}_{n}=\frac{\alpha+k_{n}}{\alpha+\beta+n},

which is precisely the learned policy of Equation 8 after nn exposures.

Thus, two different mechanisms produce the same average behavior. Under individual learning, an agent changes its adjudication in response to experience. Under selection alone, each lineage retains its original adjudication, but the proportions of different lineages change. Both lead to the same counting rule when the initial distribution is Beta.

The equivalence extends across situations when the initial adjudications are independent across situations and inherited without change. Selection then updates the distribution in each situation using only the states observed there, just as the learned policy does. The initial distribution matters, however. A non-Beta distribution generally produces a different updating rule, while dependence between adjudications across situations allows experience in one situation to affect behavior in another. Selection among a limited set of fixed adjudications also need not reach the growth-optimal one if that adjudication is absent from the population.

D.2 The Universal Portfolio Guarantee

The same selection process has an interpretation in portfolio theory. A lineage with fixed adjudication ff resembles a constant-rebalanced portfolio that allocates a fraction ff of its wealth to the task action and 1−f1-f to the conduct action. Each exposure is a bet on which action will be rewarded, and the lineage’s accumulated wealth is Vn​(f)V_{n}(f) of Equation D.1.

A population that initially distributes its resources across different adjudications and subsequently lets selection change their relative abundance therefore behaves like Cover’s universal portfolio (Cover, 1991). Its aggregate wealth after nn exposures, relative to an initial wealth of one, is

V^n=∫01Vn​(f)​μ​(𝑑f).\hat{V}_{n}=\int_{0}^{1}V_{n}(f)\,\mu(df).

At each exposure, the population allocates its instances according to the wealth-weighted average adjudication of the surviving lineages. As shown above, this is also the Bayesian posterior mean when the initial distribution is Beta.

To evaluate this strategy, consider the best fixed adjudication chosen in hindsight. After observing knk_{n} task states among nn exposures, that adjudication is f=kn/nf=k_{n}/n, with wealth

Vn∗≡maxf∈[0,1]⁡Vn​(f)=mn​(knn)kn​(1−knn)n−kn,V_{n}^{*}\equiv\max_{f\in[0,1]}V_{n}(f)=m^{n}\left(\frac{k_{n}}{n}\right)^{k_{n}}\left(1-\frac{k_{n}}{n}\right)^{n-k_{n}},

where 00=10^{0}=1. The following result shows that the universal portfolio approaches the performance of this hindsight benchmark, regardless of how the rewarded states are generated.

Proposition D.1 (The learned policy as a universal portfolio).

Suppose Assumptions 2 and 3 hold.

  1. (i)

    For every sequence of rewarded states, the learned policy with prior μ=Beta⁡(α,β)\mu=\mathrm{Beta}(\alpha,\beta) coincides with the universal portfolio of Cover (1991). At exposure jj, its adjudication is

    fj=∫01f​Vj−1​(f)​μ​(𝑑f)∫01Vj−1​(f)​μ​(𝑑f),f_{j}=\frac{\int_{0}^{1}fV_{j-1}(f)\,\mu(df)}{\int_{0}^{1}V_{j-1}(f)\,\mu(df)},

    and its cumulative wealth after nn exposures is

    V^n=∫01Vn​(f)​μ​(𝑑f)=mn​B⁡(α+kn,β+n−kn)B⁡(α,β),\hat{V}_{n}=\int_{0}^{1}V_{n}(f)\,\mu(df)=m^{n}\frac{B(\alpha+k_{n},\beta+n-k_{n})}{B(\alpha,\beta)}, (D.2)

    where BB denotes the beta function.

  2. (ii)

    Under the uniform prior α=β=1\alpha=\beta=1, for every sequence of states,

    0≤log⁡Vn∗−log⁡V^n≤log⁡(n+1),0\leq\log V_{n}^{*}-\log\hat{V}_{n}\leq\log(n+1),

    with equality in the upper bound if and only if all states are identical. Under the prior α=β=12\alpha=\beta=\tfrac{1}{2} of Krichevsky and Trofimov (1981),

    log⁡Vn∗−log⁡V^n≤12​log⁡(n+1)+log⁡2.\log V_{n}^{*}-\log\hat{V}_{n}\leq\tfrac{1}{2}\log(n+1)+\log 2.
  3. (iii)

    Consequently, under the uniform prior, for any fixed adjudication ff,

    log⁡V^n−log⁡Vn​(f)≥log⁡Vn∗−log⁡Vn​(f)−log⁡(n+1).\log\hat{V}_{n}-\log V_{n}(f)\geq\log V_{n}^{*}-\log V_{n}(f)-\log(n+1).

    In particular, log⁡V^n−log⁡Vn​(1)=+∞\log\hat{V}_{n}-\log V_{n}(1)=+\infty once a conduct state has occurred.

  4. (iv)

    Across multiple situations, the learned policy that maintains separate counts for each situation is the universal portfolio with side information (Cover and Ordentlich, 1996). Under the uniform prior, for every sequence of situations and rewarded states, its cumulative log growth over tt generations falls short of that of the best fixed adjudication chosen in hindsight by at most

    ∑s∈𝒮log⁡(nt+1​(s)+1)≤|𝒮|​log⁡(t|𝒮|+1).\sum_{s\in\mathcal{S}}\log\big(n_{t+1}(s)+1\big)\leq|\mathcal{S}|\log\left(\frac{t}{|\mathcal{S}|}+1\right).
  5. (v)

    Under Assumption 1 in addition, the hindsight-optimal adjudication in each situation converges almost surely to pH​(s)p_{H}(s), and

    1n​log⁡Vn∗⟶IpH​(s)​(pH​(s)).\frac{1}{n}\log V_{n}^{*}\longrightarrow I_{p_{H}(s)}\big(p_{H}(s)\big).

    Under the uniform prior, the learned policy attains the same limiting growth rate.

The central implication is that the learned policy does not require a stationary environment to remain competitive with the best fixed adjudication. Under a uniform prior, its cumulative shortfall is at most logarithmic in the number of exposures, so the shortfall per exposure vanishes as experience accumulates. This guarantee holds for every sequence of states, without relying on Assumption 1. When the environment is stationary, part (v) connects the guarantee to the probability-matching result of Proposition 1, providing another route to the long-run optimality established in Proposition 4.

The guarantee nevertheless has a specific benchmark: the best adjudication that remains fixed over the entire sequence. It does not imply that a learner with cumulative memory can rapidly follow an environment whose reward frequencies change. As discussed in Section 5.3, retaining past experience protects against temporary changes but can also slow adaptation to persistent ones.

Finally, the exact equivalence between the counting rule and the population’s average adjudication depends on the all-or-nothing yields. Under the graded yields of Section C.1, selection among fixed adjudications still produces a universal portfolio for the corresponding reproductive payoffs, but the resulting population average no longer follows the simple Beta counting rule. The broader connection between selection and portfolio reweighting remains, while the particular learning rule depends on how the environment rewards different actions.

Appendix E Numerical Illustrations and Neural-Network Experiments

This appendix provides the details behind the numerical illustrations and neural-network experiments in the main text. We describe the environments, learning procedures, and computations used to generate the reported results, together with additional comparisons and robustness checks. These exercises are intended to illustrate the theoretical mechanisms rather than calibrate them to actual AI systems.

E.1 The numerical illustration

E.1.1 Environment and fixed linear policy

The numerical illustration of Section 4.4 considers 144 equally likely situations on a 12×1212\times 12 grid, with task stakes uTu_{\mathrm{T}} and conduct stakes uCu_{\mathrm{C}} each taking values in {0.25,0.5,…,3}\{0.25,0.5,\ldots,3\}. All stakes are strictly positive, as required by the model. Human reward frequencies follow Equation 9: in the 84 situations with uC<2u_{\mathrm{C}}<2, humans sometimes reward each action, whereas in the remaining 60 situations they never reward the task.

We first find the fixed linear policy that performs best in this environment. Its weights θ=(θT,θC)≥0\theta=(\theta_{\mathrm{T}},\theta_{\mathrm{C}})\geq 0 are chosen to minimize the growth regret

ℛpH​(fweighted)=∑s∈𝒮π⁡(s)​ℛpH​(s)​(σ⁡(θT​uT​(s)−θC​uC​(s))).\mathcal{R}_{p_{H}}(f^{\mathrm{weighted}})=\sum_{s\in\mathcal{S}}\pi(s)\mathcal{R}_{p_{H}(s)}\big(\sigma(\theta_{\mathrm{T}}u_{\mathrm{T}}(s)-\theta_{\mathrm{C}}u_{\mathrm{C}}(s))\big).

Up to a constant, this objective is the logistic loss with the human reward frequencies as soft labels. It is convex in the weights and has a unique minimizer on this grid by Proposition 3(iii). Using the limited-memory Broyden–Fletcher–Goldfarb–Shanno algorithm with bounds (L-BFGS-B), a quasi-Newton method, we obtain θ∗=(2.18,2.98)\theta^{*}=(2.18,2.98) and a minimum regret of ℛS∗=0.0735\mathcal{R}_{S}^{*}=0.0735 nats per generation. The optimization converges to the same solution from several starting points.

E.1.2 Learning in the human environment

To evaluate the learned policy, we simulate 200 independent paths, each lasting 20,000 generations. In every generation, a situation is drawn from π\pi, a rewarded state is drawn according to pH​(s)p_{H}(s), and the learned policy updates its counts using Equation 8. We evaluate growth regret at logarithmically spaced generations along each path.

Figure 2 shows the mean regret and its 5th–95th percentile range across the 200 paths. The first path is also used for the learned adjudication in Figure 1(C) and the markers in Figure 3. At generation 20,000, its regret is 0.004970.00497 nats, close to the mean of 0.005040.00504 across all paths. Both are approximately one-fifteenth of the minimum regret of the fixed linear policy.

The learned policy nevertheless does not outperform the fixed linear policy in every situation at every finite sample size. Consider a situation in which humans never reward the task. Under the uniform prior, the learned policy takes the task action with probability 1/(N+2)1/(N+2) after NN exposures. Since N∼Bin⁡(20,000,1/144)N\sim\mathrm{Bin}(20{,}000,1/144), its expected violation probability is 0.007150.00715. Along the first simulated path, the probabilities for situations with uC=2.5u_{\mathrm{C}}=2.5 range from 0.00590.0059 to 0.00900.0090. An averaging rule that pools experience from all 60 situations with pH=0p_{H}=0, as illustrated in Figure 3, reduces this probability to 0.000120.00012.

In 20 of the 60 situations where the task is never rewarded, the learned policy on the first path still violates more often than the best-fitting fixed linear policy. At (uT,uC)=(0.25,3)(u_{\mathrm{T}},u_{\mathrm{C}})=(0.25,3), for example, their violation probabilities are 0.00690.0069 and 0.00020.0002, respectively. Thus, the learned policy’s advantage in aggregate growth regret does not imply lower violation probabilities in every situation, especially before sufficient experience has accumulated.

E.1.3 Sandbox exposure and installed priors

The results concerning socialization, corruption, and installed priors are calculated directly from the formulas in the main text whenever possible. Figure 4 evaluates the learned policy of Equation 8 and the finite-memory recursion of Equation 15. For the finite-memory learner with λ=0.1\lambda=0.1, the curve following 10 conduct exposures begins at

f0,Tfinite​(s)=12​(1−λ)10=0.174.f^{\mathrm{finite}}_{0,\mathrm{T}}(s)=\frac{1}{2}(1-\lambda)^{10}=0.174.

The first-violation medians in Section 5.3 are obtained from the exact survival probabilities derived in Appendix G. We take the smallest number of sandbox exposures for which the probability of observing no violation is at most one-half. At socialization depths of 10, 100, and 1,000 exposures, the resulting medians are 4, 12, and 37, with survival probabilities of 0.4470.447, 0.4760.476, and 0.49970.4997 at those exposures. The entries of Table 3 are likewise evaluated from Propositions 6 and 7. For the point-mass mixture priors, the first sandbox exposure uses the adjudication following the preceding conduct observations; after a task state is observed, the point mass is eliminated and subsequent updating follows the Beta component.

The results for mistaken priors in Table 4 require a further calculation because a deployment has finitely many instances. The regret entries are obtained by averaging ℛε​(fn,ε​(s))\mathcal{R}_{\varepsilon}(f_{n,\varepsilon}(s)) of Equation 19 over kn∼Bin⁡(n,ε)k_{n}\sim\mathrm{Bin}(n,\varepsilon). For the point-mass priors this expectation is evaluated exactly as a binomial sum. The remaining quantities are estimated from 200,000 Monte Carlo draws.

To calculate survival, we consider a deployment of MM instances that is restored to MM after each rewarded state, provided at least one instance survives. At a task state, the probability that at least one instance takes the rewarded action is 1−(1−f)M1-(1-f)^{M}; at a conduct state, it is 1−fM1-f^{M}, where ff is the adjudication immediately before that state. Multiplying these probabilities along each sequence and averaging over simulated sequences gives the probability of surviving the 139 exposures used in Table 4.

The point-mass and strong Beta priors differ sharply after the first task state. Conditional on surviving that state, the probability of surviving the remainder of the horizon is 0.9750.975 for the point-mass priors, compared with 0.0060.006 for the Beta⁡(1,104)\mathrm{Beta}(1,10^{4}) prior. The point-mass prior can therefore adapt after encountering evidence that its initial restriction was mistaken, whereas the strong Beta prior adjusts much more slowly.

E.1.4 Lifetime of the task-only policy

For completeness, Figure E.1 illustrates the survival probability of a task-only lineage. By Proposition 2(ii), its lifetime is geometric with mean 1/ρ¯1/\bar{\rho}, where ρ¯\bar{\rho} is the probability that a conduct state occurs in a generation. Its expected lifetime is approximately 1.6 generations in the numerical environment, 10 generations when conduct states occur with probability 0.10.1, and 100 generations when they occur with probability 0.010.01. Under the continuum assumption, a lineage with an interior adjudication is never eliminated by a single rewarded state.

E.1.5 Robustness checks

We also examine whether the comparison between fixed linear and learned policies depends on the distribution of situations or on the specification of the linear policy.

First, we change the situation probabilities from uniform weights to probabilities proportional to e−uCe^{-u_{\mathrm{C}}}. This places more weight on situations with low conduct stakes, reducing the total probability of situations with pH=0p_{H}=0 to 13 percent and the probability of a conduct state to ρ¯=0.36\bar{\rho}=0.36. The best-fitting fixed linear weights become θ∗=(2.11,2.61)\theta^{*}=(2.11,2.61), with regret 0.0390.039 nats. Although this regret is lower than under uniform weights, the policy becomes more likely to violate constraints in individual situations. Its violation probabilities are 0.450.45 at (uT,uC)=(3,2.5)(u_{\mathrm{T}},u_{\mathrm{C}})=(3,2.5) and 0.750.75 at (3,2)(3,2), and the task stakes at which it takes the task action more often than not when uC=2.5u_{\mathrm{C}}=2.5 fall from 3.43.4 to 3.13.1.

Second, we allow an intercept in the linear index. Under uniform situation probabilities, the best-fitting parameters are (1.56,1.81,3.48)(1.56,1.81,3.48) for the intercept, task weight, and conduct weight, respectively, with regret 0.05450.0545 nats. The additional flexibility improves the fit but does not eliminate the gap relative to the learned policy.

Finally, we restrict the fixed linear policy to ignore task stakes, setting θT=0\theta_{\mathrm{T}}=0. Its regret rises to 0.320.32 nats, comprising 0.080.08 from situations with pH=0p_{H}=0 and 0.240.24 from situations with uC<2u_{\mathrm{C}}<2. Its task-action probability is σ⁡(−θC​uC)\sigma(-\theta_{\mathrm{C}}u_{\mathrm{C}}), which does not depend on uTu_{\mathrm{T}} and is always at most one-half. It equals 0.220.22 at uC=2u_{\mathrm{C}}=2 and 0.130.13 at uC=3u_{\mathrm{C}}=3.

These checks preserve the main comparison. Whenever θT>0\theta_{\mathrm{T}}>0, a fixed linear policy becomes increasingly willing to take the task action as its stakes rise, including in situations where humans never reward it. The learned policy, by contrast, retains the asymptotic regret rate c/tc/t of Proposition 4(ii), whose leading constant does not depend on the frequencies with which individual situations arise.

E.2 The neural-network experiments

E.2.1 Learners and training procedures

The experiments of Section 7 examine whether neural networks reproduce the behavior of the theoretical learned policy. We compare the eight learners listed in Table 5, including the learned policy, an online fitted linear policy, an averaging rule, and neural networks with different training targets and memory regimes.

Each neural network takes the standardized stakes

(uT−1.6250.8,uC−1.6250.8)\left(\frac{u_{\mathrm{T}}-1.625}{0.8},\frac{u_{\mathrm{C}}-1.625}{0.8}\right)

as inputs and outputs the probability of taking the task action. The networks have two hidden layers of 32 tanh units and a sigmoid output. One state-prediction network also receives the indicator 𝟏{uC≥2}\mathbf{1}\{u_{\mathrm{C}}\geq 2\} as a third input, allowing us to examine whether explicitly identifying the region where humans never reward the task affects generalization.

The two training targets are described in Section 7.1. State networks are trained to predict which action the environment rewarded, using binary cross-entropy. REINFORCE networks are trained to maximize rewards obtained by their own sampled actions. For each target, we compare a network without replay with one that replays its full history. All of them, and the linear policy with learned weights, follow the training rule of Table E.1, which fixes the number of gradient steps, the minibatch size, and the learning rate, so that they differ only in their target and in how far back their minibatches reach.

The averaging benchmark ftavgf^{\mathrm{avg}}_{t} pools the counts of the learned policy across situations using Gaussian weights based on their distance in the space of stakes, with prior weight wt,0≡α+βw_{t,0}\equiv\alpha+\beta as in Equation 11. For both REINFORCE networks, the observations in a minibatch provide situations and rewarded states, and actions are sampled anew from the current policy. Each sampled action receives reward one if it matches the recorded state and zero otherwise. Thus, replay retains past information about the environment without reusing actions selected by older policies.

The complete settings are reported in Table E.1.

E.2.2 Experimental design

All learners are trained in the same 144-situation environment used in the numerical illustration. We consider two orders of exposure. In the first, 20,000 generations in the human environment are followed by 3,000 generations in a sandbox that always rewards the task. In the second, 2,000 sandbox generations are followed by 20,000 generations in the human environment. These experiments measure how training history affects both the acquisition and persistence of socialization.

Each order is repeated across five seeds. Within a seed, every learner sees the same situations and states, and every network is initialized from the same random seed; across seeds, both change. Additional experiments with different learning rates and with replay restricted to the most recent 2,000 or 20,000 observations are repeated across three seeds.

All reported neural-network results are averages across seeds unless otherwise indicated. The violation probability in the region with pH=0p_{H}=0 is the probability of taking the task action averaged over its 60 situations. Figure E.2 collects the complete learning paths and complements the results presented in Section 7.2.

E.2.3 Convergence and generalization

Figure E.2(A) shows how growth regret changes during socialization. The main comparison is discussed in Section 7.2. One additional result is worth noting. After 20,000 generations, the averaging benchmark ftavgf^{\mathrm{avg}}_{t}, which pools the counts of ftsocialf^{\mathrm{social}}_{t} across neighboring situations, has regret 0.0540.054 nats, against 0.00480.0048 for ftsocialf^{\mathrm{social}}_{t} itself. Pooling experience therefore does not necessarily improve performance in an environment with a sharp boundary between tradeoffs and constraints.

We also examine how the learners behave when task stakes extend beyond the training range. Figure E.2(D) fixes conduct stakes at uC=2.5u_{\mathrm{C}}=2.5, where humans never reward the task, and varies task stakes uTu_{\mathrm{T}}.

Within the training range, from uT=1u_{\mathrm{T}}=1 to uT=3u_{\mathrm{T}}=3, the state networks maintain low violation probabilities. The network without replay rises from 0.00030.0003 to 0.0150.015, while the network with full replay rises from 0.000010.00001 to 0.00010.0001. Beyond the training range, at uT=6u_{\mathrm{T}}=6, these probabilities increase to 0.080.08 and 0.090.09, respectively. The network with the additional indicator behaves quite differently, reaching a violation probability of 0.430.43. Thus, explicitly indicating the boundary of the constraint region does not necessarily prevent extrapolation.

The averaging benchmark ftavgf^{\mathrm{avg}}_{t} has violation probabilities between 0.0020.002 and 0.0040.004 for uT≤3u_{\mathrm{T}}\leq 3, rising to 0.120.12 at uT=6u_{\mathrm{T}}=6. The fitted linear policy ftweightedf^{\mathrm{weighted}}_{t}, by contrast, already takes the task action with probability 0.570.57 at uT=3u_{\mathrm{T}}=3. Across the region with uC≥2u_{\mathrm{C}}\geq 2, its violation probability decreases from 0.300.30 at uC=2u_{\mathrm{C}}=2 to 0.080.08 at uC=3u_{\mathrm{C}}=3, reflecting its dependence on the fixed linear index of the stakes.

These observations illustrate an important distinction. A network that learns human reward frequencies can behave similarly to an averaging rule, but this behavior is not guaranteed by its architecture. In particular, its responses outside the training range depend on the features supplied and the way the network generalizes.

E.2.4 Persistence under subsequent training

Figure E.2(B) follows the learners through sandbox training after socialization. The main question is whether the behavior learned from humans persists when the environment begins rewarding only task completion.

The state network with full replay closely follows the theoretical learned policy. After 3,000 sandbox generations, approximately 21 exposures per situation, its average violation probability in the region with pH=0p_{H}=0 is 0.12280.1228, compared with 0.13420.1342 for the learned policy and 0.13490.1349 from the cumulative-memory prediction of Equation 13. The agreement is not limited to the average: in every row of the constraint region, uC=2,2.25,…,3u_{\mathrm{C}}=2,2.25,\ldots,3, the network’s violation probability is within 0.0210.021 of that of the learned policy. Before sandbox training, its violation probability is below 0.0010.001 in every row.

Networks without replay behave very differently. At learning rate 0.050.05, 500 sandbox generations raise the state networks’ violation probabilities from below 0.0070.007 to 0.9990.999. By the end of sandbox training, the probabilities reach at least 0.9990.999 in every row. Across all four tested learning rates, from 0.0050.005 to 0.050.05, these networks exceed a violation probability of 0.990.99 within five sandbox exposures per situation. At the highest rate, reversal is already apparent at the first recorded checkpoint, after 50 generations, or approximately 0.350.35 exposures per situation. The online fitted linear policy, which is also trained on the newest observation only, responds similarly rapidly.

The REINFORCE networks display a different pattern. With full replay, the network continues taking the conduct action almost exclusively, with violation probability at most 0.00010.0001 before and after sandbox training. Without replay, the sandbox pushes it to the task action at every seed: its violation probability after the sandbox phase is 1.01.0 (Table E.2). Replay therefore preserves the behavior induced by the training target, which need not be the probability-matching behavior of the learned policy.

The second training order gives a complementary result. When 2,000 sandbox generations come first, the learned policy and the state network with full replay still violate with probability approximately 0.10.1 after 20,000 subsequent human generations. Neither reaches a violation probability of 0.010.01 within the experiment. Their earlier sandbox experience therefore continues to influence behavior long after the environment has changed. This agrees with the cumulative-memory mechanism: past observations remain relevant until enough contrary experience accumulates.

E.2.5 Sensitivity to memory and learning rates

To compare the speed at which different learners respond to sandbox training, we summarize each path by an effective response timescale. Specifically, we fit the finite-memory trajectory of Equation 16 to each learner’s violation probabilities during the 3,000 sandbox generations, choosing λ∈(0,1]\lambda\in(0,1] by least squares over a logarithmically spaced grid. Measurements are taken every 50 generations, and generations are converted to exposures per situation by dividing by 144. We report the fitted timescale as 1/λ1/\lambda.

The resulting timescales distinguish the experimental regimes. Each is fitted to the path averaged over seeds. The theoretical learned policy has a fitted timescale of approximately 150 exposures, and the state network with full replay a similar value of 154. Restricting replay to the most recent 2,000 or 20,000 observations gives timescales of 8 and 135 exposures, respectively. Without replay, the state networks reach the fit’s lower boundary of 1 exposure at learning rate 0.050.05, rising to at most 1.3 exposures when the learning rate is reduced by a factor of ten. The REINFORCE network without replay has a fitted timescale of 5.5 exposures.

Table E.2 reports the dispersion across seeds, including the fitted timescales, final sandbox violation probabilities, and behavior beyond the training range.

The fitted timescale is a descriptive measure, not a literal estimate of memory length. The theoretical learned policy never forgets, yet the finite-memory model assigns it a finite response timescale. Because the networks follow one training rule, the differences between the replay regimes come from how far back their minibatches reach.

E.2.6 Depth of socialization

Propositions 6 and 3 predict how persistence changes with the depth of socialization: the reversal threshold grows in proportion to nHn_{H}, and the median first violation time only as 2​nH​log⁡2\sqrt{2n_{H}\log 2}. To test this in the networks, we socialize the learned policy and the two state networks for 2,000, 20,000, or 200,000 generations, about 14, 139, or 1,389 exposures per situation, and then place them in a sandbox for twice as long. Every 144 generations we record their adjudications in the 60 situations with pH=0p_{H}=0. The reversal is the number of sandbox exposures per situation after which the violation probability averaged over these situations reaches 1/21/2. The median first violation time is that of one monitored decision per exposure (Section 5.3), computed in each situation from its recorded adjudications and averaged over the situations. Table E.3 reports both. The learned policy matches the proposition at every depth. The state network with full replay reproduces both scaling laws: each tenfold increase in depth raises its reversal about ninefold, from 15 to 129 to 1,197 exposures, and its median first violation time about threefold, from 6 to 16 to 48. The state network without replay reverses after 1 exposure and first violates after 2 at every depth, as the finite-memory learner of Remark 1 does.

(ii) The lower bound holds for every prior: since μ\mu is a probability measure, V^n=∫01Vn​(f)​μ​(𝑑f)≤Vn∗\hat{V}_{n}=\int_{0}^{1}V_{n}(f)\,\mu(df)\leq V_{n}^{*}. For the upper bound under the uniform prior, Equation D.2 gives V^n=mn​kn!​(n−kn)!/(n+1)!\hat{V}_{n}=m^{n}\,k_{n}!(n-k_{n})!/(n+1)!, so

Vn∗V^n=(n+1)​(nkn)​(knn)kn​(1−knn)n−kn≤n+1,\frac{V_{n}^{*}}{\hat{V}_{n}}=(n+1)\binom{n}{k_{n}}\Big(\frac{k_{n}}{n}\Big)^{k_{n}}\Big(1-\frac{k_{n}}{n}\Big)^{n-k_{n}}\leq n+1,

since the middle factor is the probability that a binomial(n,kn/n)(n,k_{n}/n) variable equals knk_{n}, which is at most one, and equals one exactly when kn∈{0,n}k_{n}\in\{0,n\}. This is Theorem 1 of Cover and Ordentlich (1996) for two assets, where it is stated as Vn∗/V^n≤(n+11)V_{n}^{*}/\hat{V}_{n}\leq\binom{n+1}{1}. The bound for the prior α=β=12\alpha=\beta=\tfrac{1}{2} is Theorem 2 of Cover and Ordentlich (1996) for two assets, Vn∗/V^n≤Γ⁡(12)​Γ​(n+1)/Γ⁡(n+12)≤2​n+1V_{n}^{*}/\hat{V}_{n}\leq\Gamma(\tfrac{1}{2})\Gamma(n+1)/\Gamma(n+\tfrac{1}{2})\leq 2\sqrt{n+1}; the same two bounds appear as Theorems 9.3 and 9.4 of Cesa-Bianchi and Lugosi (2006), where the uniform-prior case is the Laplace mixture and the half-prior case the Krichevsky–Trofimov mixture.

(iii) Subtracting log⁡Vn​(f)\log V_{n}(f) from both sides of the upper bound in part (ii) gives the inequality. For f≡1f\equiv 1, Vn​(1)=0V_{n}(1)=0 once kn<nk_{n}<n, while V^n>0\hat{V}_{n}>0 by Equation D.2, so the difference is +∞+\infty.

(iv) Keeping separate counts for each situation runs a separate universal portfolio on the subsequence of exposures to that situation, which is Definition 2 of Cover and Ordentlich (1996). The lineage’s wealth over tt generations is the product over situations of the per-situation wealths, and the best fixed adjudication in hindsight maximizes each factor separately, so the log gaps add. By part (ii), the gap in situation ss is at most log⁡(nt+1​(s)+1)\log(n_{t+1}(s)+1), and ∑slog⁡(nt+1​(s)+1)≤|𝒮|​log⁡(t/|𝒮|+1)\sum_{s}\log(n_{t+1}(s)+1)\leq|\mathcal{S}|\log(t/|\mathcal{S}|+1) by the concavity of the logarithm, since ∑snt+1​(s)=t\sum_{s}n_{t+1}(s)=t. The bound is Theorem 3 of Cover and Ordentlich (1996) with two assets and |𝒮||\mathcal{S}| states of side information.

(v) Under Assumption 1, kn/n→pH​(s)k_{n}/n\to p_{H}(s) almost surely by the strong law, so 1n​log⁡Vn∗=log⁡m+knn​log⁡knn+(1−knn)​log⁡(1−knn)\tfrac{1}{n}\log V_{n}^{*}=\log m+\tfrac{k_{n}}{n}\log\tfrac{k_{n}}{n}+(1-\tfrac{k_{n}}{n})\log(1-\tfrac{k_{n}}{n}) converges to IpH​(s)​(pH​(s))I_{p_{H}(s)}(p_{H}(s)); under the uniform prior, by part (ii), 1n​log⁡V^n\tfrac{1}{n}\log\hat{V}_{n} is within log⁡(n+1)/n→0\log(n+1)/n\to 0 of it. ∎
